lessons.title: Ich hatte ihn schon gesehen: das Plusquamperfekt (1)
lessons.goal: Say what had already happened before another past event, using hatte plus Partizip II and signal words like schon, vorher and noch nie.

grammar.topic: Plusquamperfekt with haben: the past before the past
grammar.point: The Plusquamperfekt with haben is hatte (hatte, hattest, hatte, hatten, hattet, hatten) in position 2 plus the Partizip II at the end: Ich hatte ihn schon gesehen. The participle is the same as in the Perfekt. It names the earlier of two past events, often with schon, vorher, bereits or noch nie. The later event stays in the Präteritum or Perfekt.
grammar.oneLine: Ben hatte vorher noch nie Deutsch gelernt.

mistake.wrong: Ich habe vorher schon gegessen gehabt.
mistake.why: The Plusquamperfekt is hatte plus participle. The double form gegessen gehabt is a colloquial habit, not standard German.

terms.meaning: the past before the past: hatte or war plus a participle
a small word like schon or vorher that shows an event came first

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich habe Ben kennengelernt' to 'Ich hatte ihn schon im Kurs gesehen'
cards.body: This chapter is called Zwischenmenschliches: everything that happens between people, from friendship to love to a fight. Today Anna unpacks a box and finds an old photo. You can already say what happened. Now you learn to say what had already happened before that.
steps: You already know: Ich habe Ben in Hamburg kennengelernt. The Perfekt tells what happened.
New today: Ich hatte ihn vorher schon zweimal im Kurs gesehen. hatte plus a participle tells what happened even earlier.
By the end you can: say what had already happened before another event, with hatte plus Partizip II and small signal words like schon and vorher.

examples.de: Ich habe Ben in Hamburg kennengelernt.
examples.en: I met Ben in Hamburg.
examples.why: You know this: the Perfekt.

examples.de: Ich hatte ihn vorher schon zweimal im Kurs gesehen.
examples.en: I had already seen him twice in the course before.
examples.why: New today: the same participle, but hatte instead of habe.

cards.more: Imagine two boxes on a shelf. The first holds things that are finished: the Perfekt. Today you open a second box that sits behind it, with things that were finished even earlier, before something else happened. Only the little helper changes. Instead of habe you say hatte, and the participle stays exactly as you know it. Gesehen, gekauft and gelernt all work again. Think of hatte as a clock set one step further back.

cards.title: Old photos in a box
cards.body: Anna is packing and finds a photo from Frau Weber's course in Hamburg. Look for hatte plus a participle in the dialogue. Each time it tells you what had happened before the photo was taken. The story itself stays in the Präteritum.
cards.lead: A scene from packing day in the WG. Read it once and mark every hatte with its participle. The next cards explain why German uses this form here and how you build it.

examples.de: Er hatte vorher noch nie Deutsch gelernt!
examples.en: He had never learned German before!
examples.why: Mira says it about Ben.

examples.de: Ich hatte nur ein Buch gekauft.
examples.en: I had only bought a book.
examples.why: Ben answers.

examples.de: Ich hatte alle Wörter gelernt, aber ich verstand nichts.
examples.en: I had learned all the words, but I understood nothing.
examples.why: Hatte for the earlier part, Präteritum for the story.

deeper.text: Look at noch nie: it means never before. Ben hatte noch nie Deutsch gelernt describes how things stood when the story began. The Plusquamperfekt often sets the scene like this, and the story then moves on in the Präteritum. First the background, then the action: that is the usual order in a good story.

example.de: Ben hatte noch nie Deutsch gelernt, aber er lachte viel.
example.en: Ben had never learned German, but he laughed a lot.

cards.more: Read the dialogue like a detective. Every hatte is a clue: something happened before this moment. Ben had bought a book, Ben had learned words. Those things are over and form the background. Then look at the verbs without hatte, like verstand. They carry the story forward. So hatte plus participle answers the question: what was already true when the story began? The Präteritum answers: what happened next?
steps: Anna: Schau mal, ein Foto aus Frau Webers Kurs in Hamburg!
Mira: Ja, das ist Ben. Er hatte vorher noch nie Deutsch gelernt!
Ben: Stimmt, ich hatte nur ein Buch gekauft.
Anna: Und wie war der erste Tag?
Ben: Schrecklich! Ich hatte alle Wörter gelernt, aber ich verstand nichts.
Mira: Ich hatte schon vier Wochen lang gelernt und konnte dir helfen.
Anna: Und dann habt ihr zusammen Kaffee getrunken?
Ben: Ja, das war der Anfang.

cards.title: Two pasts on a timeline
cards.body: The Plusquamperfekt is the past before the past. You always need two events. The earlier one gets hatte plus Partizip II. The later one uses the Präteritum or the Perfekt. Without a second event there is nothing to be earlier than.
cards.lead: Now the idea behind the form. Before we build hatte plus participle, see on a timeline which event gets it: always the one that happened first.

examples.de: Ich hatte das Buch gekauft.
examples.en: I had bought the book.
examples.why: Earlier: Plusquamperfekt.

examples.de: Dann kam ich in den Kurs.
examples.en: Then I came into the course.
examples.why: Later: Präteritum.

examples.de: Ben hatte ein Buch gekauft, dann kam er in den Kurs.
examples.en: Ben had bought a book, then he came to the course.
examples.why: Both events in one sentence pair.

deeper.text: In everyday speech many people use the Plusquamperfekt rarely. They say vorher and the Perfekt instead. In stories, reports and written texts the Plusquamperfekt is normal and shows the order exactly. Both are correct. You need to understand hatte plus participle, and you can use it when the order matters.

example.de: Ich habe vorher schon gegessen.
example.en: I have already eaten before.

cards.more: Think of a film with a flashback. The main film runs in the Präteritum: Ben kam in den Kurs. Then the film jumps back to show what had happened before, like a short clip: Er hatte ein Buch gekauft. That clip is the Plusquamperfekt. When the clip ends, the film goes on in the Präteritum again. Only the flashback gets hatte plus participle. Everything on the main line stays simple.
steps: 1  Earlier: Ich hatte das Buch gekauft. (Plusquamperfekt)
2  Later: Dann kam ich in den Kurs. (Präteritum)
3  Now: Heute spreche ich Deutsch.

cards.title: The forms of hatte
cards.body: hatte is the Präteritum of haben, so you already know it. Take the right form for the subject and put it in position 2. The Partizip II stands at the very end. The participle never changes, only hatte does.
cards.lead: This is the engine of the whole lesson: hatte in all six persons. Learn the table once, because every sentence in this chapter uses one of these forms.

examples.de: Du hattest das Foto gemacht.
examples.en: You had taken the photo.
examples.why: du: hattest.

examples.de: Anna hatte die Kartons gepackt.
examples.en: Anna had packed the boxes.
examples.why: er/sie/es: hatte, without ending.

examples.de: Ihr hattet den Kurs bezahlt.
examples.en: You (all) had paid for the course.
examples.why: ihr: hattet.

examples.de: Wir hatten Kaffee getrunken.
examples.en: We had drunk coffee.
examples.why: wir: hatten.

deeper.text: Be careful with hatte and hätte. One umlaut changes the meaning: Ich hatte Zeit means I had time, Ich hätte Zeit means I would have time. You know hätte from the dream sentences in chapter 4. Later you will meet the longer form hätte plus participle. Today just notice the difference when you read, and never mix the two when you write.

example.de: Gestern hatte ich keine Zeit.
example.en: Yesterday I had no time.
example.why: hatte, no umlaut: a real past.

cards.more: Think of hatte as a chameleon, just like the Präteritum you already know. With ich and er it is hatte, with du it adds -st, with wir and sie -n, with ihr -t. The participle is the quiet partner at the end of the sentence. It does not change for any person. So if you know six forms of hatte and your participles, you can say everything. Practise it out loud with the same participle and six different people.
steps: 1  Pick the form of hatte for your subject.
2  Put it in position 2.
3  Put the Partizip II at the very end.

cards.title: Which participle? The same as in the Perfekt
cards.body: You do not learn new participles. The Partizip II is exactly the one from the Perfekt: gekauft, gesehen, eingekauft, studiert, verstanden. Only the helper changes from habe or hast to hatte or hattest.
cards.lead: Good news first: no new forms to memorise. This card shows that each type of participle you know from the Perfekt works unchanged in the Plusquamperfekt.

examples.de: Leon hatte im Supermarkt eingekauft.
examples.en: Leon had gone shopping in the supermarket.
examples.why: separable: ein-ge-kauft.

examples.de: Herr Ali hatte in Zürich gekocht.
examples.en: Herr Ali had cooked in Zürich.
examples.why: regular: ge-...-t.

examples.de: Ben hatte den Satz nicht verstanden.
examples.en: Ben had not understood the sentence.
examples.why: inseparable: no ge-.

examples.de: Mira hatte Frau Weber schon getroffen.
examples.en: Mira had already met Frau Weber.
examples.why: irregular: ge-...-en, vowel change.

deeper.text: Mixed verbs change the vowel and still end in -t: bringen, gebracht, denken, gedacht, kennen, gekannt. In the Plusquamperfekt they work just the same. If you are unsure about a participle, look it up in the Perfekt column of your verb list. Whatever you find there, you can keep, and you only swap the helper.

example.de: Ben hatte ein Geschenk mitgebracht.
example.en: Ben had brought a present.

cards.more: Imagine a sandwich. The helper is the top slice and the participle is the bottom slice, and the middle is the story. In the Perfekt the top slice is habe. In the Plusquamperfekt you swap it for hatte, and the bottom slice stays the same. Regular verbs end in -t, strong verbs end in -en, separable verbs keep the ge- in the middle, and -ieren verbs have no ge- at all. Swap one slice and you are done.

cards.title: Signal words: schon, vorher, bereits, noch nie
cards.body: Small words show that something is earlier: schon, vorher, bereits, noch nie, kurz davor. They usually stand in the middle of the sentence, between hatte and the participle. They are not required, but they make the order very clear.
cards.lead: Now the little helpers that tell your listener that an event came first. They sit in the middle of the sentence, and you will hear them in almost every story.

examples.de: Herr Ali hatte vorher in Zürich gearbeitet.
examples.en: Herr Ali had worked in Zürich before.
examples.why: vorher: before.

examples.de: Ich hatte noch nie so viel gelacht.
examples.en: I had never laughed so much before.
examples.why: noch nie: never before.

examples.de: Anna hatte bereits alle Kartons gepackt.
examples.en: Anna had already packed all the boxes.
examples.why: bereits: already, a bit formal.

examples.de: Kurz davor hatte es geregnet.
examples.en: Just before, it had rained.
examples.why: kurz davor: just before that.

deeper.text: Bereits means the same as schon, but it sounds more formal and is more common in writing. In a message to a friend you write schon. In a letter to a company or in a news report you often read bereits. Zuvor is similar: it means before and belongs mostly in written German. Choose the word that matches the situation.

example.de: Der Kurs hatte bereits begonnen.
example.en: The course had already begun.

cards.more: Signal words are like road signs. Schon and bereits say: this was already finished. Vorher and zuvor say: this came first. Noch nie says: there was no earlier time. Kurz davor says: this was close to the other event. They usually stand after hatte, before the participle, so the sentence still has the shape hatte, something, participle. With them, your listener can follow the order even if the tenses sound similar.

rows: Herr Ali hatte vorher in Zürich gearbeitet.
Ich hatte noch nie so gelacht.

cards.title: Perfekt or Plusquamperfekt?
cards.body: One past event alone: use the Perfekt or Präteritum. Two past events where one was earlier: put the earlier one in the Plusquamperfekt. Do not overuse it. If the order is already clear from dann or danach, the simple past is enough.
cards.lead: The last question is when to use it. This card gives you a quick rule of thumb, so that you use the Plusquamperfekt where it helps and not everywhere.

examples.de: Gestern habe ich Ben getroffen.
examples.en: Yesterday I met Ben.
examples.why: One event: Perfekt.

examples.de: Ich hatte Ben schon getroffen. Dann lud ich ihn ein.
examples.en: I had already met Ben. Then I invited him.
examples.why: Two events: the earlier one gets hatte.

examples.de: Ich kam nach Hause, und Anna hatte schon gekocht.
examples.en: I came home and Anna had already cooked.
examples.why: The order matters here, so hatte helps.

deeper.text: English says had done much more often than German says hatte gemacht. When the order is clear, German is happy with the Präteritum: Ich kam nach Hause und aß etwas. Use the Plusquamperfekt only for the part that came first and that would be unclear otherwise. A long chain of hatte sentences sounds heavy. One or two are enough.

example.de: Ich kam nach Hause und aß etwas.
example.en: I came home and ate something.
example.why: Order is clear: simple past is enough.

cards.more: Imagine you tell a story to a friend. You do not repeat had every time in German. You set the earlier event once with hatte, and then you go on in the Präteritum. If the second event follows with dann or danach, you may not need the Plusquamperfekt at all. It is a tool for unclear order, not a rule you must apply to every sentence. Ask yourself: would the listener lose the order without it?

rows: Ich kam nach Hause und aß etwas.

lessons.title: Er war gerade angekommen: das Plusquamperfekt (2)
lessons.goal: Use war plus Partizip II, put the helper last in als-, weil- and dass-clauses, and tell a story with the Plusquamperfekt.

grammar.topic: Plusquamperfekt with sein and in side clauses
grammar.point: For verbs of movement and change (kommen, fahren, umziehen, bleiben, passieren, sein) the Plusquamperfekt is war plus Partizip II: Er war gerade erst aus Madrid gekommen. The choice of haben or sein is the same as in the Perfekt. In side clauses hatte or war stands last: …, weil er den Bus verpasst hatte. Reflexive verbs keep sich after the helper: Sie hatten sich kennengelernt.
grammar.oneLine: Als Mira in die WG kam, war Leon schon eingezogen.

mistake.wrong: Als Mira kam, hatte Leon schon eingezogen.
mistake.right: Als Mira kam, war Leon schon eingezogen.
mistake.why: einziehen is a change of place, so it takes sein, like in the Perfekt: Leon ist eingezogen.

terms.meaning: hatte or war, the verb before the participle
a clause with als, weil or dass: the finite verb stands last

cards.title: Before we start: from 'hatte gekauft' to 'war gekommen'
cards.body: Last time you learned hatte plus a participle. But in the Perfekt some verbs take sein: Ben ist nach Hamburg gekommen. The Plusquamperfekt follows the same rule. For those verbs the earlier past gets war plus Partizip II. Today you learn the second helper.
steps: You already know: Ben hatte noch nie Deutsch gelernt. hatte plus a participle for most verbs.
New today: Ben war gerade erst aus Madrid gekommen. war plus a participle for verbs of movement and change.
By the end you can: choose hatte or war, put the helper last in a side clause, and tell a classic too-late story.

examples.de: Ben hatte noch nie Deutsch gelernt.
examples.en: Ben had never learned German.
examples.why: You know this: hatte plus participle.

examples.de: Ben war gerade erst aus Madrid gekommen.
examples.en: Ben had only just come from Madrid.
examples.why: New today: war plus participle.

cards.more: Think of the Perfekt for a moment. Some verbs say ich habe, and others say ich bin. The choice depends on the verb, not on the tense. The Plusquamperfekt keeps exactly the same choice and only moves everything one step back: habe becomes hatte, and bin becomes war. So you do not learn a new rule today. You learn a second helper and apply the old rule to it.

cards.title: Ben's story
cards.body: Here is Ben's story, told from today. Some sentences use hatte, others war. Read it and ask for each verb: is it a movement or a change of state? Then it takes war. Is it an action? Then it takes hatte. The main story stays in the Präteritum.
cards.lead: Before the rules, read a short story with both helpers in it. Ben's first days in Hamburg give you six sentences to spot war and hatte.

examples.de: Er war gerade erst aus Madrid gekommen.
examples.en: He had only just come from Madrid.
examples.why: kommen: change of place, so war.

examples.de: Am ersten Kurstag kam er zu spät, denn er hatte den Bus verpasst.
examples.en: On the first course day he was late, because he had missed the bus.
examples.why: verpassen: an action, so hatte.

examples.de: Mira war schon zwei Wochen im Kurs gewesen.
examples.en: Mira had already been in the course for two weeks.
examples.why: sein itself: war gewesen.

deeper.text: Look at the participle of sein: gewesen. It takes sein as its helper, so you get war gewesen. That looks like a double word, but it is perfectly regular: Mira war schon zwei Wochen im Kurs gewesen means she had already been there for two weeks. You will meet it in many stories, so learn war gewesen as one pair.

example.de: Ben war noch nie in Deutschland gewesen.
example.en: Ben had never been in Germany.
example.why: war gewesen: the pair for had been.

cards.more: This story has two layers. The top layer is the Präteritum: kam, gingen, erzählte. These sentences move the story forward. The bottom layer is the Plusquamperfekt: war gekommen, hatte verpasst, war gewesen. These sentences look back and explain. When you read the story, you can mentally colour the two layers differently. Then you see that the explaining layer uses hatte for actions and war for movements and changes.
steps: Im September kam Ben zum ersten Mal in Frau Webers Kurs.
Er war gerade erst aus Madrid gekommen.
Am ersten Kurstag kam er zu spät, denn er hatte den Bus verpasst.
Mira war schon zwei Wochen im Kurs gewesen.
Nach dem Kurs gingen sie in ein Café.
Dort erzählte Ben von Madrid.

cards.title: war plus participle: the forms
cards.body: war is the Präteritum of sein. Use it with the Partizip II of verbs of movement (kommen, fahren), change of state (umziehen) and of bleiben, passieren and sein. It is the same choice as in the Perfekt: ist gekommen becomes war gekommen.
cards.lead: Now the forms. Learn war in all six persons, and keep in mind that the participle comes from the Perfekt and never changes.

examples.de: Ich war nach Berlin gefahren.
examples.en: I had gone to Berlin.
examples.why: fahren: movement.

examples.de: Wir waren zu spät gekommen.
examples.en: We had come too late.
examples.why: wir: waren.

examples.de: Was war passiert?
examples.en: What had happened?
examples.why: passieren: sein, always.

examples.de: Sie waren nach Wien umgezogen.
examples.en: They had moved to Wien.
examples.why: umziehen: change of place.

deeper.text: Be careful with ihr wart. It has no e. It is the ihr-form of war, you were. Do not confuse it with ihr wartet, the present of warten, you wait. One letter and one sound change the meaning completely: Ihr wart pünktlich means you were on time, but Ihr wartet auf den Bus means you are waiting for the bus.

example.de: Ihr wart schon gegangen.
example.en: You (all) had already left.

cards.more: Imagine a coin with two sides. One side says hatte, the other says war. You flip it by asking one question about the verb: does it describe an action done to something, or a movement and change of the subject itself? Movement and change land on war: gefahren, gekommen, geblieben, passiert. Everything else lands on hatte. The coin works the same way in the Perfekt, so you flip it with a skill you already own.
steps: 1  Is it movement, change of state, bleiben, passieren or sein? Then war.
2  Is it an action? Then hatte.
3  Put the participle at the very end.

cards.title: hatte or war? Sort the verbs
cards.body: Same verb family, different helper: einziehen takes war, einrichten takes hatte. A verb of changing place or state takes war. A verb that does something to an object takes hatte. When you are unsure, ask which helper the Perfekt uses.
cards.lead: The hardest part is choosing between hatte and war. This card puts pairs of similar verbs next to each other so that you see the difference quickly.

examples.de: Leon war schon eingezogen.
examples.en: Leon had already moved in.
examples.why: einziehen: he changes place.

examples.de: Leon hatte das Zimmer eingerichtet.
examples.en: Leon had furnished the room.
examples.why: einrichten: an action on an object.

examples.de: Anna war früh aufgestanden.
examples.en: Anna had got up early.
examples.why: aufstehen: change of state.

examples.de: Anna hatte die Küche aufgeräumt.
examples.en: Anna had tidied the kitchen.
examples.why: aufräumen: an action on an object.

deeper.text: In Austria and southern Germany some verbs take sein where northern Germany uses haben: sitzen, stehen and liegen. People there say ich bin gesessen. So Mira from Wien can say Ich war gesessen, while standard German has Ich hatte gesessen. Recognise the southern form when you hear it, but write the standard form in tests.

example.de: Ich hatte lange gesessen.
example.en: I had been sitting for a long time.

cards.more: Imagine you are a bouncer at two doors. At the war door you let in verbs where the subject itself moves or changes: einziehen, aufstehen, ankommen. At the hatte door you let in verbs where somebody does something to something: einrichten, aufräumen, anrufen. The prefix does not decide. Ein- and auf- appear on both doors. Only the meaning counts. If the subject moves or changes, it is war; if the subject acts on an object, it is hatte.

cards.title: In a side clause: the helper goes last
cards.body: In a side clause with als, weil or dass the finite verb stands at the very end. In the Plusquamperfekt that is hatte or war. The participle stands right before it: …, weil er den Bus verpasst hatte. In the main clause war and hatte stay in position 2.
cards.lead: Now word order in longer sentences. The helper moves to the very end of a side clause, and the participle waits just in front of it.

examples.de: Als Mira in die WG kam, war Leon schon eingezogen.
examples.en: When Mira came into the flat, Leon had already moved in.
examples.why: als-clause first: the main clause starts with its verb.

examples.de: Ben kam zu spät, weil er den Bus verpasst hatte.
examples.en: Ben came late because he had missed the bus.
examples.why: weil: the helper hatte is last.

examples.de: Leon sagte, dass er schon gegessen hatte.
examples.en: Leon said that he had already eaten.
examples.why: dass: the same shape.

deeper.text: If the side clause comes first, the main clause begins with its verb: Weil er den Bus verpasst hatte, kam er zu spät. After the comma the verb takes position 1 and the subject follows. This is the same rule you know from all side clauses. The Plusquamperfekt just makes the end of the clause two words long: participle plus helper.

example.de: Weil er den Bus verpasst hatte, kam er zu spät.
example.en: Because he had missed the bus, he came late.
example.why: Side clause first: then the main verb comes next.

cards.more: Picture the side clause as a small suitcase that is packed in a fixed order: conjunction, subject, the details, then the participle, and finally the helper like a lock on the lid. In a main clause the helper sits in the second seat, but in a side clause it jumps to the very last seat. The participle is the passenger who sits just before it. If the side clause comes first in the sentence, the main clause starts with its verb.
steps: 1  Main clause: Leon war schon eingezogen. (war in position 2)
2  Side clause: …, weil er den Bus verpasst hatte. (hatte last)
3  Participle right before the helper: verpasst hatte.

cards.title: Reflexive and separable verbs
cards.body: Reflexive and separable verbs work as always. The reflexive pronoun follows hatte or war directly after a pronoun subject: Sie hatten sich kennengelernt. A separable verb has ge- inside the participle: anschauen becomes angeschaut. The helper still decides the tense.
cards.lead: Two types of verbs behave a little differently in the sentence. This card shows how the pronoun sich and the separable prefix fit in.

examples.de: Sie hatten sich auf einer Party kennengelernt.
examples.en: They had got to know each other at a party.
examples.why: sich kennenlernen: reflexive, written as one word in the participle.

examples.de: Mira hatte sich sehr gefreut.
examples.en: Mira had been very happy.
examples.why: sich freuen: haben.

examples.de: Anna hatte sich schon im Mai entschieden.
examples.en: Anna had already decided in May.
examples.why: sich entscheiden: no ge-.

examples.de: Leon hatte die Wohnung schon angeschaut.
examples.en: Leon had already looked at the flat.
examples.why: separable: an-ge-schaut.

deeper.text: Reflexive verbs are the favourite verbs for first meetings: sich kennenlernen, sich verlieben, sich treffen. Note that kennenlernen is written as one word in the participle, kennengelernt, and the ge- sits inside. Ben and Anna have a favourite joke about their first meeting: Liebe auf den ersten Blick? Nein, auf den zweiten! They had not noticed each other the first time.

example.de: Sie hatten sich zuerst kaum beachtet.
example.en: At first they had hardly noticed each other.
example.why: sich beachten: they ignored each other.

cards.more: Reflexive verbs have a little partner: sich. In the Plusquamperfekt the partner sits right behind the helper, like a shadow behind a person. The helper still sits in position 2 and the participle at the end, and sich fits in between them. With separable verbs the prefix does not split off: it stays inside the participle, in the middle. So the sentence shape does not change: subject, hatte, sich, details, participle.

cards.title: The classic too-late story
cards.body: The classic story: Als ich am Bahnhof ankam, war der Zug schon abgefahren. The als-clause says what happened later (Präteritum). The main clause tells what was already finished (Plusquamperfekt), usually with schon. You can use it for trains, films and shops.
cards.lead: Now you can tell a whole little story. The too-late story is the best example, because the order of events is the point of the story.

examples.de: Als ich am Bahnhof ankam, war der Zug schon abgefahren.
examples.en: When I arrived at the station, the train had already left.
examples.why: The classic too-late story.

examples.de: Als Anna nach Hause kam, hatte Leon schon gekocht.
examples.en: When Anna came home, Leon had already cooked.
examples.why: Action: hatte.

examples.de: Als wir ankamen, hatte der Film schon angefangen.
examples.en: When we arrived, the film had already begun.
examples.why: anfangen: hatte.

deeper.text: Gerade erst means only just. It makes the earlier event very close to the later one. Als Mira ankam, hatte Ben gerade erst angefangen means Ben had started only a moment before she came. You can also use it for people: Wir hatten uns gerade erst kennengelernt, so we had only just met. A useful little phrase for first meetings.

example.de: Wir hatten uns gerade erst kennengelernt.
example.en: We had only just met.

cards.more: Tell the story in three beats. Beat one: you arrive (als-clause in the Präteritum). Beat two: you discover that something was already over (main clause with war or hatte plus schon). Beat three: you react in the Präteritum again. The surprise lives in beat two, and the Plusquamperfekt is the word that creates it. Without it the sentence would only report; with it, the listener hears that you came too late.
steps: 1  Als-clause, the later event: Als ich ankam, …
2  Main clause, the earlier event: …war der Zug schon abgefahren.
3  Add schon or gerade erst to show the order.

lessons.title: Freunde fürs Leben: Freundschaftsgeschichten
lessons.goal: Understand and tell friendship stories with the Präteritum and Plusquamperfekt, and match information to short texts.

grammar.topic: Friendship stories with Präteritum and Plusquamperfekt
grammar.point: Tell a friendship story with the Präteritum (or Perfekt) for what happened and the Plusquamperfekt for what had happened before: Wir hatten uns auf einer Party kennengelernt. Von da an haben wir uns oft getroffen. Say ein Freund von mir for a friend who is not a partner, because mein Freund usually means boyfriend.
grammar.oneLine: Wir hatten uns aus den Augen verloren.

mistake.wrong: Er ist mein Freund, aber wir sind nicht zusammen.
mistake.right: Er ist ein Freund von mir.
mistake.why: mein Freund usually means boyfriend or partner. For a friend who is not a partner, say ein Freund von mir.

terms.meaning: an exam task where you connect statements to texts
a different word with the same meaning

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ben hatte noch nie Deutsch gelernt' to whole friendship stories
cards.body: You can now say what had happened before another event. Today you use that skill for something bigger: telling how a friendship began. You also read short texts about friends and learn to match them to tasks, which is a typical exam task at B1.
steps: You already know: Wir hatten uns auf einer Party kennengelernt. A single earlier event.
New today: Wir sind seit zwanzig Jahren befreundet. Wie hat alles angefangen? A whole story with background and action.
By the end you can: describe a good friend, match information to short texts, and tell your own friendship story.

examples.de: Wir hatten uns auf einer Party kennengelernt.
examples.en: We had met at a party.
examples.why: You know this: one earlier event.

examples.de: Wir sind seit zwanzig Jahren befreundet.
examples.en: We have been friends for twenty years.
examples.why: New today: a friendship that lasts.

examples.de: Wie hat alles angefangen?
examples.en: How did it all begin?
examples.why: New today: the question for the story.

cards.more: There is no new grammar in this lesson, and that is on purpose. You already own the tools: the Präteritum for the story and the Plusquamperfekt for the background. Today you put them to work. A friendship story is the perfect test, because it always has a before and an after: how we lived before, how we met, and what happened next. If the tenses feel natural by the end, you are ready.

cards.title: What makes a good friend?
cards.body: Good friends are ehrlich, zuverlässig, hilfsbereit and treu. You can trust them (man kann ihnen vertrauen) and tell them a secret (ein Geheimnis anvertrauen). These words are the base for every friendship text in this lesson.
cards.lead: First the vocabulary of friendship. Learn these qualities as a small word map, because the texts and the exam tasks that follow use them all the time.

examples.de: Ein guter Freund ist ehrlich und zuverlässig.
examples.en: A good friend is honest and reliable.
examples.why: Two qualities with und.

examples.de: Man kann ihm ein Geheimnis anvertrauen.
examples.en: You can entrust him with a secret.
examples.why: anvertrauen: dative plus accusative.

examples.de: Anna ist treu und hilfsbereit.
examples.en: Anna is loyal and helpful.
examples.why: Treu for people.

deeper.text: Treu is used for friends, for partners and also for customers: treue Kunden are customers who come back year after year. In all cases it means that someone stays with you even when things get difficult. It is a strong word, so Germans use it less casually than English speakers use loyal. For everyday kindness, hilfsbereit or nett is more common.

example.de: Herr Ali hat viele treue Kunden.
example.en: Herr Ali has many loyal customers.
example.why: Treu is not only for friends.

cards.more: Make a word map in your head with Freund in the middle and four arms. One arm is honesty: ehrlich. One is reliability: zuverlässig, verlässlich. One is helping: hilfsbereit. One is staying: treu. Then add two phrases on the side: jemandem vertrauen and ein Geheimnis anvertrauen. When a text describes a friend, look for the arm it belongs to. That tells you the quality even if you do not know every word.

rows: Sie bleibt auch in schweren Zeiten.

cards.title: Four short texts: Meine beste Freundschaft
cards.body: A newsletter asks readers: Meine beste Freundschaft. Four people answer. Read each text once for the general idea. Notice how each uses the Präteritum for the story and the Plusquamperfekt for what was earlier, for example hatte gearbeitet.
cards.lead: Time to read real stories. Each of the four texts is about 55 words. Read them one after another, and see the Präteritum and Plusquamperfekt do their jobs together.

examples.de: Als ihre Familie in eine andere Stadt zog, schrieben wir uns Briefe.
examples.en: When her family moved to another city, we wrote each other letters.
examples.why: Frau Weber: the Präteritum carries the story.

examples.de: In Zürich hatte ich in einem Hotel gearbeitet.
examples.en: In Zürich I had worked in a hotel.
examples.why: Herr Ali: the Plusquamperfekt gives the background.

examples.de: Seine Mutter hatte immer Pasta gekocht.
examples.en: His mother had always cooked pasta.
examples.why: Leon: hatte plus participle again.

deeper.text: Notice the little phrase wir kannten uns nur vom Sehen in the last text. It means we only knew each other by sight. It is a great phrase for people you see often but have never really talked to. Many friendships start there. And notice the last sentence: aus einer Nachbarschaft kann eine Freundschaft werden, so a friendship can grow out of a neighbourhood.

example.de: Wir kannten uns nur vom Sehen.
example.en: We only knew each other by sight.

cards.more: Read each text like a small film. First the situation at the start, then the turning point, then how things are today. In the first text the turning point is the move to another city. In the second it is the move to Berlin. In the third it is that they now see each other only in summer. In the fourth it is the broken bicycle. Find the turning point and you understand the whole story.
steps: Frau Weber: Meine Schulfreundin und ich saßen in der Schule nebeneinander. Als ihre Familie in eine andere Stadt zog, schrieben wir uns jahrelang Briefe. Später hatten wir beide ein Handy, und wir telefonierten jeden Sonntag. Wir haben uns nie aus den Augen verloren, auch nicht nach dreißig Jahren. Das ist Freundschaft.

Herr Ali: In Zürich hatte ich in einem Hotel gearbeitet, und dort lernte ich einen Kollegen kennen. Er war Koch wie ich. Wir hielten zusammen, wenn die Arbeit schwer war. Als ich nach Berlin zog, hatten wir Angst, dass wir den Kontakt verlieren würden. Aber wir rufen uns bis heute jede Woche an. Das ist Treue.

Leon: Mein bester Freund lebt in Italien. Wir kennen uns aus dem Kindergarten und waren als Kinder jeden Tag zusammen. Ich war oft bei ihm, und seine Mutter hatte immer Pasta gekocht. Heute sehen wir uns nur im Sommer, aber wir schreiben uns jeden Abend eine Nachricht. Das ist uns wichtig.

Eine Nachbarin: Mein Fahrrad war kaputt, als ich im Repair-Café eine Frau aus meinem Haus traf. Wir kannten uns nur vom Sehen. Sie reparierte mein Fahrrad, und ich brachte ihr Kuchen mit. Jetzt trinken wir jeden Freitag zusammen Kaffee. So kann aus einer guten Nachbarschaft eine Freundschaft werden. Ich bin sehr froh darüber.

cards.title: Strategy: match information to texts
cards.body: In a matching task you get several texts and several statements. Read the statements first. Underline the key words. Then look in the texts for synonyms, not for the same words. Check names and numbers. One text may fit no statement.
cards.lead: Now the exam strategy. Matching tasks are a standard part of the B1 reading exam, and a clear routine makes them much easier than they look.

examples.de: Wir telefonierten jeden Sonntag.
examples.en: We phoned every Sunday.
examples.why: The statement says regelmäßig Kontakt: a synonym.

examples.de: Wir sehen uns nur im Sommer.
examples.en: We only see each other in summer.
examples.why: The statement says selten: a synonym.

examples.de: Mein Fahrrad war kaputt.
examples.en: My bicycle was broken.
examples.why: The statement says Reparatur: a hint.

examples.de: Sie reparierte mein Fahrrad.
examples.en: She repaired my bicycle.
examples.why: The same idea in a different word.

deeper.text: In the Goethe B1 reading exam, part three works like this: there are more statements or advertisements than people, so some of them stay unused. That is why you must never force a match. If a statement fits no text, mark it as unused and move on. Also watch out for traps: a text may contain the same word as a statement and still mean something different.

example.de: Es gibt mehr Texte als Aufgaben.
example.en: There are more texts than tasks.

cards.more: Think of matching as a game of finding twins. Each statement has at most one twin text, and the twins never wear exactly the same clothes: the statement says regelmäßig, the text says jeden Sonntag. So you hunt for the same meaning in other words. Names and numbers are the fastest clues, because they cannot be disguised. When you find a twin, cross it out. What remains gets easier with every match.
steps: 1  Read the statements first.
2  Underline the key words.
3  Look in the texts for synonyms, not for the same words.
4  Check names and numbers.
5  One text can fit no statement: do not force a match.

cards.title: Kinds of friends: Freund or Freund von mir?
cards.body: German has several words: der beste Freund, die beste Freundin, der Kumpel (informal), der Bekannte, der Freundeskreis. Be careful: mein Freund often means boyfriend. To say a friend who is not a partner, say ein Freund von mir.
cards.lead: The word Freund can cause a real misunderstanding. This card sorts the words for different kinds of friends and shows the safe way to say that someone is just a friend.

examples.de: Das ist ein Freund von mir.
examples.en: That is a friend of mine.
examples.why: Safe: friend, not partner.

examples.de: Ben ist mein bester Freund.
examples.en: Ben is my best friend.
examples.why: With bester it is clear.

examples.de: Sie ist eine gute Bekannte von uns.
examples.en: She is a good acquaintance of ours.
examples.why: Less close than a friend.

deeper.text: With the possessive, mein Freund or meine Freundin usually suggests a partner. That is why many people add a word to be clear: ein guter Freund, ein Freund von mir, ein alter Freund. In a group, Freundeskreis means the whole circle of friends. And der Kumpel is a mate you do things with, like football, but it is informal and mostly used by men.

example.de: Er ist ein guter Freund von mir.
example.en: He is a good friend of mine.

cards.title: Telling your friendship story
cards.body: A friendship story has three parts: how it began, what had happened before, and how it is now. Ask Wie habt ihr euch eigentlich kennengelernt? and answer with the Plusquamperfekt for the background and the Präteritum or Perfekt for the story.
cards.lead: This last card puts it all together. It gives you a model for telling your own friendship story, and the question your friends will ask you.

examples.en: How did you actually meet?

examples.why: Background in the Plusquamperfekt.

deeper.text: Two fixed phrases are worth learning by heart. Freunde fürs Leben means friends for life, and durch dick und dünn gehen means to go through thick and thin, which is to stay together in good and bad times. Both are used for very close friendships, and both sound natural in a toast or a birthday card. You can also hear Seitdem sind wir unzertrennlich: since then we have been inseparable.

example.de: Die beiden sind durch dick und dünn gegangen.
example.en: The two of them went through thick and thin.

cards.more: Imagine a story in three little boxes. In box one you put the background: Wir hatten uns aus den Augen verloren. In box two you put the turning point: Dann habe ich sie zufällig getroffen. In box three you put today: Jetzt sind wir wieder befreundet. Each box has its own tense. If you fill the three boxes in this order, your listener always knows where in time you are, and your story sounds clear and natural.

Wir hatten uns auf einer Party kennengelernt.

lessons.title: Nachdem ich angekommen war, …: nachdem und die Zeitenfolge
lessons.goal: Connect two events in order with nachdem and choose the right tenses: Plusquamperfekt before Präteritum, Perfekt before Präsens.

grammar.topic: nachdem and the sequence of tenses
grammar.point: Nachdem opens a clause with the verb at the end. The clause names the earlier event, so its tense is one step further back than the main clause: Plusquamperfekt (hatte/war + Partizip II) → main clause in Präteritum or Perfekt; Perfekt → main clause in Präsens or Futur. If the nachdem clause comes first, the main verb follows right after the comma.
grammar.oneLine: Nachdem er angekommen war, suchte er eine Wohnung.

mistake.wrong: Nachdem er kam nach Berlin, hatte er eine Wohnung gesucht.
mistake.right: Nachdem er nach Berlin gekommen war, suchte er eine Wohnung.
mistake.why: The first event goes into the nachdem clause in the Plusquamperfekt with the verb at the end. The second event is the main clause in the Präteritum.

terms.meaning: the sequence of tenses: which tense goes in which clause when two events follow each other
a clause that cannot stand alone; the finite verb is at the end: …, nachdem er angekommen war.

cards.title: Before we start: from two sentences to one with nachdem
cards.body: Herr Ali tells his life as a story. You already say what happened first with hatte plus participle. Today you join two events into one sentence with nachdem (after) and choose the right tense on each side. Our story is how he came to Berlin.
steps: You already know: Herr Ali hatte in Zürich als Koch gearbeitet. Dann kam er nach Berlin.
New today: one sentence with nachdem: Nachdem er in Zürich gearbeitet hatte, kam er 2001 nach Berlin.
By the end you can: link two events with nachdem and pick the right tenses (Plusquamperfekt before Präteritum, Perfekt before Präsens).

examples.de: Herr Ali hatte in Zürich als Koch gearbeitet.
examples.en: Mr Ali had worked as a cook in Zürich.
examples.why: You know this: the earlier event with hatte + participle.

examples.de: Dann kam er 2001 nach Berlin.
examples.en: Then he came to Berlin in 2001.
examples.why: You know this: the later event in the Präteritum.

examples.de: Nachdem er in Zürich als Koch gearbeitet hatte, kam er 2001 nach Berlin.
examples.en: After he had worked in Zürich as a cook, he came to Berlin in 2001.
examples.why: New today: both events in one sentence.

examples.de: Nachdem Leon gekocht hatte, spülte Mira das Geschirr.
examples.en: After Leon had cooked, Mira washed the dishes.
examples.why: New today: the same pattern with other people.

cards.more: Picture two boxes. Box one holds what happened first, box two holds what happened next. Before today you put each box into its own sentence and wrote Dann between them. Now nachdem is the glue that ties box one to box two. The glue always sits in front of the earlier box, and that box ends with hatte or war. You will meet this pattern in every story where one thing follows another, in speech as well as in writing.

cards.title: Herr Ali's way to Berlin
cards.body: Herr Ali tells his story in order: Zürich, then Berlin in 2001, then a kitchen, then his own restaurant. Each step starts with nachdem and the step before. The nachdem clause is always the earlier event and ends with hatte or war. The main clause says what came next.
cards.lead: Read the whole story once before we study the rule. Look at each nachdem clause: it tells the step before and ends with hatte or war, and the main clause tells what happened next.

examples.de: Nachdem er in Zürich gearbeitet hatte, kam er 2001 nach Berlin.
examples.en: After he had worked in Zürich, he came to Berlin in 2001.

examples.de: Nachdem er in Berlin angekommen war, arbeitete er zuerst in einer fremden Küche.
examples.en: After he had arrived in Berlin, he first worked in someone else's kitchen.

examples.de: Nachdem er einige Jahre gespart hatte, eröffnete er das Restaurant „Zum Löwen“.
examples.en: After he had saved for a few years, he opened the restaurant „Zum Löwen“.

deeper.text: Herr Ali tells the story in the Präteritum because it reads like a text. In a chat he would keep the nachdem clause and put the main clause into the Perfekt: Nachdem er in Zürich gearbeitet hatte, ist er nach Berlin gekommen. The earlier event stays in the Plusquamperfekt, only the later event changes its form.

example.de: Nachdem er gespart hatte, hat er das Restaurant eröffnet.
example.en: After he had saved, he opened the restaurant.

cards.more: Think of dominoes standing in a row. The first domino falls and pushes the second. In Herr Ali's life the first domino is Zürich, the second is Berlin, the third is the kitchen and the fourth is the restaurant. Each nachdem clause names the domino that has already fallen, and the main clause names the one that falls next. If you can line up the dominoes in the right order, the German sentence builds itself.
steps: Zürich: Herr Ali hatte als Koch gearbeitet.
2001: Er kam nach Berlin.
Berlin: Er arbeitete in einer fremden Küche.
Später: Er eröffnete „Zum Löwen“.

cards.title: nachdem sends the verb to the end
cards.body: Nachdem works like weil and dass: the conjunction opens the clause, the subject follows and the finite verb goes to the very end. In the Plusquamperfekt that is the participle, then hatte or war. If the nachdem clause comes first, the main verb stands right after the comma.
cards.lead: The story used nachdem again and again. Now you look at its word order: where the verb goes inside the clause, and what happens to the verb of the main clause that follows it.

examples.de: Nachdem Herr Ali angekommen war, suchte er eine Wohnung.
examples.en: After Mr Ali had arrived, he looked for a flat.

examples.de: Nachdem Mira gegessen hatte, ging sie in ihr Zimmer.
examples.en: After Mira had eaten, she went to her room.

examples.de: Nachdem Ben den Kurs besucht hatte, sprach er besser Deutsch.
examples.en: After Ben had attended the course, he spoke better German.

deeper.text: The order of the two parts is free. You can also start with the main clause: Herr Ali suchte eine Wohnung, nachdem er angekommen war. Now the later event comes first in the sentence, but the nachdem clause still holds the earlier event. Both versions say the same thing; in the second one the comma comes before nachdem and no verb jumps up.

example.de: Herr Ali suchte eine Wohnung, nachdem er angekommen war.
example.en: Mr Ali looked for a flat after he had arrived.

cards.more: Compare a train. The nachdem clause is a short train with the engine at the back: the verb comes last, hatte or war. The main clause is a second train that starts at the platform. When the nachdem train drives first, the next train starts with its engine, so the verb stands right after the comma: war, suchte er. When the nachdem train drives second, the main clause goes first and is perfectly normal.

cards.title: The tense sequence: the core rule
cards.body: The nachdem clause is always one step further back than the main clause. Past story: Plusquamperfekt after nachdem, Präteritum or Perfekt in the main clause. Present or future: Perfekt after nachdem, Präsens or Futur in the main clause.
cards.lead: Now the core rule. Two small tables show which tense goes in the nachdem clause and which in the main clause, for a story in the past and for a routine or plan.

examples.de: Nachdem Mira gegessen hatte, ging sie in ihr Zimmer.
examples.en: After Mira had eaten, she went to her room.

examples.de: Nachdem Mira gegessen hatte, ist sie in ihr Zimmer gegangen.
examples.en: After Mira had eaten, she went to her room.

examples.de: Nachdem ich gegessen habe, spüle ich das Geschirr.
examples.en: After I have eaten, I wash the dishes.

examples.de: Nachdem Leon gekocht hat, räumt er die Küche auf.
examples.en: After Leon has cooked, he tidies the kitchen.

deeper.text: In everyday talk many Germans use the Perfekt in both parts: Nachdem ich gegessen habe, bin ich gegangen. You will hear this often and it is not shocking. But in exams, in writing and in careful speech, a story in the past wants the Plusquamperfekt in the nachdem clause: Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, bin ich gegangen. Use the rule from the table and you are always correct.

example.de: Nachdem ich gegessen hatte, bin ich gegangen.
example.en: After I had eaten, I left.

cards.more: Always ask: which event is further back? The nachdem clause is the event that happened first, so its tense is one step back from the main clause. If the main clause is in the past, you go back once more and need hatte or war. If the main clause is now or in the future, the Perfekt is enough, because the Perfekt looks back from the present. So the tense of the main clause tells you the tense of the nachdem clause.

rows: Nachdem er angekommen war, suchte er eine Wohnung.
Nachdem ich gegessen habe, spüle ich ab.

cards.title: First event first: how to check
cards.body: Test every sentence in three steps: first find out which event happened first, then put that event into the nachdem clause, then choose the tense from the table. Never put the later event into the nachdem clause, and never use the same tense in both parts in writing.
cards.lead: You know the rule. This card gives you a small routine to build your own nachdem sentence from two events without guessing, and warns about the typical mistake of the same tense in both parts.

examples.de: Nachdem Ben aus Madrid gekommen war, lernte er Deutsch.
examples.en: After Ben had come from Madrid, he learned German.

examples.de: Nachdem Anna ihre Kisten gepackt hatte, rief sie Mira an.
examples.en: After Anna had packed her boxes, she called Mira.

examples.de: Nachdem Leon gegessen hat, lernt er für die Uni.
examples.en: After Leon has eaten, he studies for university.

deeper.text: Some words make the sequence even tighter: kurz nachdem (shortly after), gleich nachdem (right after), erst nachdem (only after). They stand in front of nachdem and change nothing in the grammar: Gleich nachdem Mira nach Hause gekommen war, rief sie Ben an. The tense rule stays exactly the same.

example.de: Gleich nachdem Mira nach Hause gekommen war, rief sie Ben an.
example.en: Right after Mira had come home, she called Ben.

cards.more: Imagine a very short film in two scenes. In scene one something happens, in scene two the next thing happens. You pick scene one first and give it to nachdem, then write scene two as the main clause. The mistake happens when the scenes get mixed up: Nachdem er ankam, hatte er gesucht tells the film backwards. If you always start with scene one, your tenses fall into place without effort.
steps: 1. Which event happened first? That one goes into the nachdem clause.
2. Is the story in the past? Then use hatte or war + participle at the end.
3. Is it a routine or a plan? Then use habe, hast or hat + participle at the end.
4. The main clause tells the second event: Präteritum or Perfekt (past), Präsens or Futur (now).

cards.title: nach dem or nachdem?
cards.body: You know nach dem Umzug: nach + dative + noun, no verb of its own. Nachdem ich umgezogen war is a clause with its own subject and verb at the end. So: a noun after nach dem, a whole clause after nachdem. Both mean the same, but nachdem needs a subject and a verb.
cards.lead: You already use nach with a noun. This card compares it with nachdem, so you know when a noun is enough and when you need a whole clause with a tense.

examples.de: Nach dem Umzug suchte Anna ein Atelier.
examples.en: After the move Anna looked for a studio.

examples.de: Nachdem Mira, Ben und Anna nach Berlin gezogen waren, suchten sie eine Wohnung.
examples.en: After Mira, Ben and Anna had moved to Berlin, they looked for a flat.

examples.de: Nach dem Essen spülen wir.
examples.en: After the meal we wash up.

examples.de: Nachdem wir gegessen haben, spülen wir.
examples.en: After we have eaten, we wash up.

deeper.text: There is also the adverb danach. It is a normal word in the main clause, so the verb stays in second place: Herr Ali kam nach Berlin. Danach suchte er eine Wohnung. After danach the verb comes at once, with no comma jump and no verb at the end. Only nachdem sends the verb to the end of its clause.

example.de: Danach suchte er eine Wohnung.
example.en: After that he looked for a flat.

cards.more: Look at what comes after the little word. After nach dem you find a noun with an article: der Umzug, das Essen. After nachdem you find a subject and a verb that ends the clause: ich umgezogen war. The first is a snapshot, the second is a small sentence. If you want to say who did what, or you need a tense, you need nachdem. If a noun already says it all, nach dem is shorter. Danach stands alone.

rows: Nach dem Umzug suchte Anna ein Atelier.
Nachdem sie umgezogen war, suchte Anna ein Atelier.

cards.title: Anna's plan for Wien
cards.body: Anna talks about her plan. The plan lies in the future, so the nachdem clause takes the Perfekt and the main clause takes the Präsens: Nachdem ich in Wien angekommen bin, rufe ich euch an. The Perfekt shows that the first action is finished before the second starts.
cards.lead: Now you use nachdem for something that has not happened yet. Anna's plan shows the second pair of the table: Perfekt after nachdem, Präsens in the main clause.

examples.de: Nachdem ich in Wien angekommen bin, rufe ich euch an.
examples.en: After I have arrived in Vienna, I will call you.

examples.de: Nachdem ich das Atelier gesehen habe, schreibe ich Mira.
examples.en: After I have seen the studio, I will write to Mira.

examples.de: Nachdem ich meine Kisten ausgepackt habe, male ich ein neues Bild.
examples.en: After I have unpacked my boxes, I will paint a new picture.

deeper.text: With a plan, German speakers prefer the Präsens in the main clause: Nachdem ich angekommen bin, rufe ich an. The Futur is correct, too, but it sounds heavy: Nachdem ich angekommen bin, werde ich euch anrufen. You only need the Futur when you want to stress the promise or the prediction. Normally the Präsens plus a time word is enough.

example.de: Nachdem ich angekommen bin, werde ich euch anrufen.
example.en: After I have arrived, I will call you.

cards.more: Anna stands in the future and looks back at a moment that has not happened yet. She says: first this will be finished, then that. The Perfekt in the nachdem clause is her way of saying that the first thing is already done when the second begins. English does it differently and says After I arrive. German needs the Perfekt. If you keep this picture in mind, you will not mix up Präsens and Perfekt.
steps: Anna: Nachdem ich in Wien angekommen bin, rufe ich euch an.
Mira: Und wann schreibst du uns?
Anna: Nachdem ich das Atelier gesehen habe, schreibe ich dir.
Ben: Schön! Nachdem du ausgepackt hast, besuche ich dich.

lessons.title: Bevor Anna geht, …: bevor und bis
lessons.goal: Say what happens before something and until something: bevor and bis as conjunctions, and vor and bis with a noun.

grammar.point: Bevor (before) and bis (until) open a clause with the verb at the end. Both parts usually have the same tense. If the clause comes first, the main verb follows the comma directly. A noun needs the preposition: vor dem Essen, bis zum Sommer. A clause needs the conjunction: bevor wir essen, bis er kommt.
grammar.oneLine: Bevor ich fahre, packe ich meine Koffer.

mistake.wrong: Bevor ich fahre, ich packe meine Koffer.
mistake.right: Bevor ich fahre, packe ich meine Koffer.
mistake.why: If the bevor clause comes first, it is position one. The main verb must follow right after the comma, before the subject.

terms.meaning: a connecting word that opens a clause: bevor, bis, nachdem
a word before a noun: vor dem Essen, bis zum Sommer

cards.title: Before we start: from 'vor der Abfahrt' to 'bevor sie abfährt'
cards.body: Anna leaves for Vienna in March. Before she goes, she has a long to-do list. You already say vor der Abfahrt and bis zum Sommer with a noun. Today the same ideas become whole clauses: bevor (before) and bis (until), each with the verb at the end.
steps: You already know: Vor dem Umzug packt Anna. Ben bleibt bis zum Sommer in Berlin.
New today: Bevor Anna nach Wien fährt, verkauft sie ihr Fahrrad. Ben bleibt in Berlin, bis er fertig ist.
By the end you can: use bevor and bis with a clause, tell them apart from vor and bis plus noun, and turn nachdem into bevor.

examples.de: Vor dem Umzug packt Anna.
examples.en: Before the move Anna packs.
examples.why: You know this: vor + dative + noun.

examples.de: Ben bleibt bis zum Sommer in Berlin.
examples.en: Ben stays in Berlin until summer.
examples.why: You know this: bis zum + noun.

examples.de: Bevor Anna nach Wien fährt, verkauft sie ihr Fahrrad.
examples.en: Before Anna goes to Vienna, she sells her bike.
examples.why: New today: bevor opens a clause, verb last.

examples.de: Ben bleibt in Berlin, bis er fertig ist.
examples.en: Ben stays in Berlin until he is finished.
examples.why: New today: bis opens a clause, verb last.

cards.more: A noun after vor or bis is a snapshot: Vor der Abfahrt, bis zum Sommer. It tells when, but not who does what. A clause tells the whole scene: who, what and when. If you want to say who is leaving or who is finished, the noun is not enough and you need a clause. Bevor and bis are exactly the small words that open such a clause, and they push the verb to the end, like weil and nachdem.

cards.title: Anna's to-do list before Wien
cards.body: Anna writes a list of everything that must happen before she leaves. Each point becomes a sentence with bevor: the bevor clause says what comes later, the main clause says what has to happen first. The verb of the bevor clause is at the end.
cards.lead: Anna's list shows bevor at work. Read the points and see which action is in the bevor clause (the later one) and which is in the main clause (the earlier one).

examples.de: Bevor Anna nach Wien fährt, verkauft sie ihr Fahrrad.
examples.en: Before Anna goes to Vienna, she sells her bike.

examples.de: Bevor sie fährt, muss sie ihr Zimmer untervermieten.
examples.en: Before she goes, she has to sublet her room.

examples.de: Bevor Anna fährt, sortiert sie alte Kleider aus.
examples.en: Before Anna goes, she sorts out old clothes.

examples.de: Bevor sie abfährt, verschenkt sie ihre Bücher.
examples.en: Before she leaves, she gives away her books.

deeper.text: A to-do list uses infinitives: Fahrrad verkaufen, Zimmer untervermieten, Koffer packen. In a sentence you need a conjugated verb, so verkaufen becomes verkauft. Order words help: zuerst, dann, zuletzt. Zuletzt gibt sie Frau Weber den Schlüssel. Zuletzt is an adverb, so the verb stays in second place.

example.de: Zuletzt gibt sie Frau Weber den Schlüssel.
example.en: Last of all she gives Frau Weber the key.

cards.more: Think of a checklist at the airport. Every item has a tick, and the last item is the flight itself. The flight is the bevor part: it comes later and stands in the bevor clause. Everything on the list happens before it and stands in the main clause. So you can write the list in any order and still say bevor ich fahre, and the listener knows that the flight is the final point.
steps: Fahrrad verkaufen
Zimmer untervermieten
Alte Kleider aussortieren
Bücher verschenken
Zuletzt: Koffer packen und fahren

cards.title: bevor: verb last, same tense
cards.body: Bevor opens a clause and sends the finite verb to the end, like weil and nachdem. Both parts usually use the same tense: Präsens with Präsens, Präteritum with Präteritum. The bevor clause can come first or second. If it comes first, the main verb stands right after the comma.
cards.lead: You saw bevor in Anna's list. Now look at its word order and tense, and at the two possible positions of the bevor clause.

examples.de: Bevor ich fahre, packe ich meine Koffer.
examples.en: Before I leave, I pack my suitcases.

examples.de: Ich packe meine Koffer, bevor ich fahre.
examples.en: I pack my suitcases before I leave.

examples.de: Bevor Anna nach Wien fuhr, verkaufte sie ihr Fahrrad.
examples.en: Before Anna went to Vienna, she sold her bike.

deeper.text: In older or written German you also find ehe with the same meaning and the same word order: Ehe er ging, trank er einen Kaffee. Ehe sounds old-fashioned, so you only need to recognise it. In your own sentences use bevor, which is normal in speech and in writing and works exactly like ehe.

example.de: Ehe er ging, trank er einen Kaffee.
example.en: Before he left, he drank a coffee.

cards.more: Imagine the bevor clause as a short waiting room at the end of a corridor. The clause begins with bevor, the subject comes in, and the verb walks to the very end and waits there: bevor ich fahre. After the comma the main clause starts fresh with its verb in first position: packe ich. The tense is the same in both rooms, because both things belong to the same time, now or in the past.

rows: Bevor ich fahre, packe ich meine Koffer.
Ich packe meine Koffer, bevor ich fahre.
Bevor Anna fuhr, verkaufte sie ihr Fahrrad.

cards.title: bevor and nachdem: one story, two views
cards.body: The same story can be told with nachdem or with bevor. With nachdem the earlier event is in the clause; with bevor the later event is in the clause. Compare: Nachdem sie gepackt hatte, fuhr sie. = Bevor sie fuhr, packte sie. Same facts, different starting point.
cards.lead: You know nachdem from the last lesson. Here you compare it with bevor: the facts stay the same, but the clause now holds the other event and the tenses change.

examples.de: Nachdem sie gepackt hatte, fuhr sie.
examples.en: After she had packed, she left.

examples.de: Bevor sie fuhr, packte sie.
examples.en: Before she left, she packed.

examples.de: Nachdem Herr Ali gespart hatte, eröffnete er das Restaurant.
examples.en: After Mr Ali had saved, he opened the restaurant.

examples.de: Bevor Herr Ali das Restaurant eröffnete, sparte er einige Jahre.
examples.en: Before Mr Ali opened the restaurant, he saved for a few years.

deeper.text: Bevor often comes with noch, especially in advice and imperatives: Bevor du gehst, trink noch einen Kaffee! Noch adds the idea of one more thing before the moment. The word order does not change: the verb of the bevor clause is last and the imperative stands right after the comma.

example.de: Bevor du gehst, trink noch einen Kaffee!
example.en: Before you go, have one more coffee!

cards.more: Look at the same road from two ends. Standing at the start you say: after I have packed, I leave. Standing at the finish you say: before I leave, I pack. The road does not change, only your standpoint. With nachdem the first event wears the verb at the end and needs hatte or war. With bevor the later event wears the verb at the end, and both parts keep the same simple tense.

rows: Nachdem sie gepackt hatte, fuhr sie.
Nachdem er gespart hatte, eröffnete er.

cards.title: bis: until
cards.body: Bis as a conjunction means until. It opens a clause with the verb at the end and says when something stops: Ben bleibt in Berlin, bis er fertig ist. Wir warten, bis du kommst. The main clause names an action that lasts, and the bis clause names the moment it ends.
cards.lead: Bevor says what comes first. Bis does something different: it marks the end of a time that lasts. Look at what kind of action stands in the main clause.

examples.de: Ben bleibt in Berlin, bis er fertig ist.
examples.en: Ben stays in Berlin until he is finished.

examples.de: Wir warten, bis du kommst.
examples.en: We wait until you come.

examples.de: Anna malt, bis es dunkel wird.
examples.en: Anna paints until it gets dark.

examples.de: Mira lernt, bis sie müde ist.
examples.en: Mira studies until she is tired.

deeper.text: A negative idea like not before needs another word. Erst wenn means only when: Ich gehe erst, wenn du kommst, which says I will not go before you come. You do not need to produce it yet, but you should recognise it: erst shows that the moment has not come before, and wenn starts the clause.

example.de: Ich gehe erst, wenn du kommst.
example.en: I will go only when you come.

cards.more: Think of a bar of chocolate in your hand. You eat and eat, and you stop at the moment when the bar is finished. The eating is the long action in the main clause, and the moment it ends is the bis clause. Bis answers the question: until when? So use it with actions that last, like warten, bleiben, lernen, malen. For one-point actions like anrufen, bevor is the natural word.

cards.title: Preposition or conjunction?
cards.body: Vor and bis can be followed by a noun or by a whole clause. A noun needs vor + dative or bis (zum) + noun. A clause needs bevor or bis plus a verb at the end. So: vor dem Essen, but bevor wir essen. Bis Montag and bis zum Sommer, but bis er kommt.
cards.lead: Two small words each have a short and a long form. This table shows how to choose: look at what follows, a noun or a clause with its own verb.

examples.de: Vor der Abfahrt packt Anna.
examples.en: Before the departure Anna packs.

examples.de: Bevor Anna abfährt, packt sie.
examples.en: Before Anna leaves, she packs.

examples.de: Ben bleibt bis zum Sommer.
examples.en: Ben stays until summer.

examples.de: Ben bleibt, bis es Sommer wird.
examples.en: Ben stays until it becomes summer.

deeper.text: Bis also joins other words into set phrases. Bis dahin means until then and works as an adverb phrase in the main clause, so the verb comes second: Bis dahin muss alles fertig sein. You will often hear it with Bis bald and Bis morgen: those are bis plus a time word, without zu and without article.

example.de: Bis dahin muss alles fertig sein.
example.en: Until then everything must be finished.

cards.more: Ask yourself one question: is there a verb after the little word? If you hear only a noun, like der Abfahrt or dem Sommer, you have a preposition: vor, bis zu. If you hear a subject and a verb, like Anna abfährt or es Sommer wird, you have a conjunction: bevor, bis. The words vor and bevor belong together, and so do bis zum and bis. The verb is your detector. Bis is the same word in both forms; only what follows changes.

cards.title: bis or bevor? Use them in Anna's plan
cards.body: Choose bis for the end of a time that lasts: Anna wohnt in Berlin, bis sie nach Wien fährt. Choose bevor for what comes first: Bevor sie nach Wien fährt, feiert sie ein Fest. Bis answers until when, bevor answers what comes first.
cards.lead: Now you use both words in Anna's plan. For every sentence ask whether the main clause is a long action that ends (bis) or something that has to come first (bevor).

examples.de: Anna wohnt in Berlin, bis sie nach Wien fährt.
examples.en: Anna lives in Berlin until she goes to Vienna.

examples.de: Bevor Anna nach Wien fährt, feiert sie ein Fest.
examples.en: Before Anna goes to Vienna, she has a party.

examples.de: Leon kocht, bis alle satt sind.
examples.en: Leon cooks until everyone is full.

examples.de: Anna ruft Frau Weber an, bevor sie abfährt.
examples.en: Anna calls Frau Weber before she leaves.

deeper.text: English until with a negative is a trap. Ich kann nicht kommen, bis ich fertig bin sounds wrong in German. Say what you really mean: Ich kann erst kommen, wenn ich fertig bin, or use bevor with nicht. Bis needs a long action that ends. Not coming is not an action that ends, so erst wenn is the better choice.

example.de: Ich kann erst kommen, wenn ich fertig bin.
example.en: I can only come when I am finished.

cards.more: Picture a rope and a knot. The rope is a long action: warten, bleiben, malen, wohnen. Bis marks the end of the rope. The knot is a single moment: anrufen, abfahren, essen. Bevor puts the knot in front of another moment on the timeline. So if you wait, stay or work for a while, use bis. If you want to say what has to be done first, use bevor. The pair of questions until when and what first helps you choose.
