lessons.title: Seitdem ich das weiß, …: seit(dem), während, als und wenn
lessons.goal: Say since when and at the same time with seitdem and während, choose als or wenn, and use the whole set of time words.

grammar.topic: seit(dem) and während as conjunctions; als and wenn
grammar.point: Seit and seitdem (since) and während (while) open a clause with the verb at the end. Seitdem: Präsens in the main clause if the situation still continues. Während: two actions at the same time. Als is for one time in the past, wenn for repeated events, the present and the future. Seit dem Umzug and während des Kurses use a noun; seitdem ich umgezogen bin and während ich reise use a clause.
grammar.oneLine: Seitdem Anna sich entschieden hat, packt sie jeden Abend.

mistake.wrong: Wenn ich letztes Jahr in Wien war, habe ich viel gesehen.
mistake.right: Als ich letztes Jahr in Wien war, habe ich viel gesehen.
mistake.why: One single time in the past needs als, not wenn.

terms.meaning: a connecting word that opens a clause: seitdem, während, als, wenn
a word that stands alone in the main clause, with the verb in second place: Seitdem kocht er.

cards.title: Before we start: from 'seit dem Umzug' to whole clauses with seitdem and während
cards.body: You already say seit dem Umzug and während des Kurses with a noun. Today you add the long forms: seitdem and während followed by a subject and a verb at the end. You also revise als and wenn and get one overview of all time words from this chapter.
steps: You already know: Seit dem Umzug wohnen wir zusammen. Während des Kurses macht Ben Notizen.
New today: Seitdem Anna sich entschieden hat, packt sie jeden Abend. Während Anna in Wien ist, gießt Frau Weber ihre Pflanzen.
By the end you can: say since when and while with a clause, choose between als and wenn, and use the whole set of time words.

examples.de: Seit dem Umzug wohnen wir zusammen.
examples.en: Since the move we have lived together.
examples.why: You know this: seit + dative.

examples.de: Während des Kurses macht Ben Notizen.
examples.en: During the course Ben takes notes.
examples.why: You know this: während + genitive.

examples.de: Seitdem Anna sich entschieden hat, packt sie jeden Abend.
examples.en: Since Anna has decided, she packs every evening.
examples.why: New today: seitdem opens a clause, verb last.

examples.de: Während Anna in Wien ist, gießt Frau Weber ihre Pflanzen.
examples.en: While Anna is in Vienna, Frau Weber waters her plants.
examples.why: New today: während opens a clause, too.

cards.more: A noun after seit or während is a short label: seit dem Umzug, während des Kurses. It gives the time but no actors. With a clause you give the whole scene: who decided, who is away, who does what meanwhile. Seitdem and während are the small words that open such a clause. Like bevor, bis and nachdem they send the verb to the end, so you only learn the idea once for all five.

cards.title: seit and seitdem: since then until now
cards.body: Seit and seitdem start a clause that says since when something has been true. The verb stands at the end. The main clause usually stays in the Präsens, because the situation still continues: Seitdem ich in Berlin wohne, koche ich mehr. Seit and seitdem mean the same here.
cards.lead: Anna decided to go to Vienna, and since then life in the flat has changed. Look at which tense the main clause has when something started in the past and still goes on.

examples.de: Seitdem ich in Berlin wohne, koche ich mehr.
examples.en: Since I have lived in Berlin, I cook more.

examples.de: Seit ich Leon kenne, esse ich gern Pasta.
examples.en: Since I have known Leon, I like to eat pasta.

examples.de: Seitdem Anna sich entschieden hat, packt sie jeden Abend.
examples.en: Since Anna has decided, she packs every evening.

examples.de: Leon kocht mehr, seit er im Kochkurs ist.
examples.en: Leon cooks more since he has been in the cooking course.

deeper.text: Seitdem can also stand alone as an adverb at the start of a main clause. Then it is a normal word and the verb stays in second place: Seitdem kocht er jeden Abend. There is no verb at the end and no comma jump. Seitdem as conjunction opens a clause, seitdem as adverb points back to something you have just said.

example.de: Seitdem kocht er jeden Abend.
example.en: Since then he has cooked every evening.

cards.more: Imagine a stopwatch. At some moment it starts: Anna decides, you move to Berlin. The watch is still running, so German uses the Präsens for what is true now. Seit and seitdem tell you where the watch started. The clause names the starting point, often with the Perfekt for a finished event (entschieden hat) or with the Präsens for a state (wohne). The main clause tells what is true while the stopwatch runs.

cards.title: während: two things at the same time
cards.body: Während as a conjunction means while: two actions happen at the same time. It opens a clause with the verb at the end, usually in the same tense in both parts. You already know während plus genitive with a noun: während des Kurses. With a clause you need a subject and a verb: während Anna packt.
cards.lead: Now two things go on together. Look at how während joins two actions, and how this differs from während plus noun in the genitive, which you know from earlier.

examples.de: Während Anna packt, kocht Leon.
examples.en: While Anna packs, Leon cooks.

examples.de: Während Anna in Wien ist, gießt Frau Weber ihre Pflanzen.
examples.en: While Anna is in Vienna, Frau Weber waters her plants.

examples.de: Mira lernt, während Leon kocht.
examples.en: Mira studies while Leon cooks.

examples.de: Während des Kurses macht Ben Notizen.
examples.en: During the course Ben takes notes.

deeper.text: Während has a second meaning: whereas, used to show a contrast between two people or things. Mira ist ruhig, während Leon laut ist. Nothing happens at the same time here; the two parts are compared. The word order is exactly the same, so you only have to know that the sentence compares two sides.

example.de: Mira ist ruhig, während Leon laut ist.
example.en: Mira is quiet, whereas Leon is loud.

cards.more: Think of a split screen. On the left Anna packs, on the right Leon cooks, and both run at the same moment. Während is the line in the middle of the screen. Both parts keep the same tense, because both actions belong to the same time. If you only want to name the other activity, you can use während plus a noun in the genitive: während des Packens. If you want to say who does it, you need a clause.

rows: Während des Kurses macht Ben Notizen.

cards.title: als or wenn? A short review
cards.body: Als is for one time in the past: Als Mira ein Kind war, wohnte sie in Wien. Wenn is for every time (immer wenn), for the present and for the future: Immer wenn Leon kocht, singt er. Wann is only for questions: Wann kommt der Zug?
cards.lead: You met als and wenn in A2. Here is a short review, because they belong to the same family as the new time words. Ask: one time in the past, or repeated, present, future?

examples.de: Als Mira ein Kind war, wohnte sie in Wien.
examples.en: When Mira was a child, she lived in Vienna.

examples.de: Immer wenn Leon kocht, singt er.
examples.en: Whenever Leon cooks, he sings.

examples.de: Wenn Anna in Wien ankommt, ruft sie an.
examples.en: When Anna arrives in Vienna, she will call.

examples.de: Wann kommt der Zug?
examples.en: When does the train come?

deeper.text: Wenn is also right for one event in the future: Wenn Anna in Wien ankommt, ruft sie an. The future is not a single event in the past, so als is not possible. The rule is simple: als only for one event in the past. All other cases use wenn, even if it happens only once, as long as it has not happened yet.

example.de: Wenn Anna in Wien ankommt, ruft sie an.
example.en: When Anna arrives in Vienna, she will call.

cards.more: Imagine a photo album and a calendar. Als opens the photo album: one picture from the past, fixed and finished, like Als ich in Wien war. Wenn opens the calendar: things that repeat every week, things that are true now and things that will happen. Wann is the question you write on the calendar: when exactly? So when you are not sure, ask yourself whether you could put the moment in a photo album as a single picture.

cards.title: The big time overview
cards.body: You now know the full set of time clauses. Bevor: before. Nachdem: after. Während, als, wenn: at the same time. Seit and seitdem: since. Bis: until. All send the verb to the end. If the clause comes first, the main verb stands right after the comma.
cards.lead: This card puts all the time words of the chapter into one picture, ordered by time: earlier, at the same time, later, since and until. Every word has one tense tip.

examples.de: Bevor Anna fährt, packt sie.
examples.en: Before Anna leaves, she packs.

examples.de: Nachdem sie gepackt hatte, fuhr sie.
examples.en: After she had packed, she left.

examples.de: Während Anna packt, kocht Leon.
examples.en: While Anna packs, Leon cooks.

examples.de: Ben bleibt in Berlin, bis er fertig ist.
examples.en: Ben stays in Berlin until he is finished.

deeper.text: A useful small word is sobald, which means as soon as: Sobald ich ankomme, rufe ich an. It works like wenn, but stresses that the second thing follows immediately. Recognise it when you read or hear it; in your own sentences wenn is enough.

example.de: Sobald ich ankomme, rufe ich an.
example.en: As soon as I arrive, I will call.

cards.more: Think of a timeline with a marker for now. Bevor points to a moment later than the main clause, nachdem to a moment earlier. Während, als and wenn sit on the same spot. Seit and seitdem point from the past to now, and bis points from now to a future end. If you draw this line once on paper and write the words on it, you will find the right word whenever you need it.

rows: Nachdem sie gepackt hatte, fuhr sie.
Seitdem ich hier wohne, koche ich mehr.
Ben bleibt, bis er fertig ist.

cards.title: Anna's last week: a time sequence
cards.body: To tell a week in order, combine the sequence words zuerst, dann, danach, schließlich with the clauses of this chapter. The adverbs keep the verb in second place; the conjunctions send it to the end. Mixed together they make a text that is easy to follow.
cards.lead: Here is a short text about Anna's last week. Notice how adverbs and conjunctions alternate, and where the verb stands after each of them.

examples.de: Zuerst verkauft Anna ihr Fahrrad.
examples.en: First Anna sells her bike.

examples.de: Danach sortiert sie ihre Kleider aus.
examples.en: After that she sorts out her clothes.

examples.de: Bevor sie fährt, feiert sie ein Fest.
examples.en: Before she leaves, she has a party.

examples.de: Schließlich gibt sie Frau Weber den Schlüssel.
examples.en: In the end she gives Frau Weber the key.

deeper.text: Endlich and schließlich are not the same. Endlich means at last and shows relief after waiting: Endlich sind die Koffer gepackt! Schließlich means in the end, as the final step of a series: Schließlich gibt sie Frau Weber den Schlüssel. Use endlich for a feeling, schließlich for the last point in a list.

example.de: Endlich sind die Koffer gepackt!
example.en: At last the suitcases are packed!

cards.more: Imagine you are the film director of Anna's week. Adverbs are the cuts between scenes: zuerst, danach, schließlich. Conjunctions are the scenes that overlap: während Anna packt, kocht Leon. If you only use adverbs, the film is a plain list. If you add a bevor or a nachdem here and there, the scenes connect, and the listener sees how the week hangs together. Try to switch between both tools.
steps: Zuerst verkauft Anna ihr Fahrrad.
Danach sortiert sie ihre Kleider aus.
Während sie packt, kocht Leon für alle.
Bevor sie fährt, feiert die WG ein Abschiedsfest.
Schließlich gibt sie Frau Weber den Ersatzschlüssel.

cards.title: Preposition, conjunction or adverb?
cards.body: Seit, während and bis each have a short form with a noun and a long form with a clause. Seit dem Umzug, seitdem ich umgezogen bin. Während der Reise, während ich reise. Seitdem can also be an adverb alone: Seitdem wohne ich hier. Look at what follows.
cards.lead: Most time words in this chapter exist in three forms. This table shows the three jobs side by side, so you can see in a second which one you need.

examples.de: Seit dem Umzug wohnen wir zusammen.
examples.en: Since the move we have lived together.

examples.de: Seitdem wir umgezogen sind, wohnen wir zusammen.
examples.en: Since we moved, we have lived together.

examples.de: Seitdem wohnen wir zusammen.
examples.en: Since then we have lived together.

examples.de: Während der Reise schläft Ben.
examples.en: During the trip Ben sleeps.

deeper.text: In spoken German you often hear während dem Essen with the dative instead of the genitive. It is common, but still counts as colloquial. In writing and in exams use the genitive: während des Essens. As a conjunction there is no case at all, because a clause follows: während wir essen.

example.de: Während des Essens telefoniert niemand.
example.en: During the meal nobody makes phone calls.

cards.more: Look at the three jobs like three different tools in a toolbox. The preposition is a small screwdriver for a noun: seit dem Umzug. The conjunction is a pair of pliers that holds two whole clauses together: seitdem ich umgezogen bin. The adverb is a marker pen that points to something already said: seitdem. All three carry the same idea of since, but each fits only one kind of job. After the word, check: noun, clause or nothing?

lessons.title: Es gibt Streit in der WG: über Konflikte sprechen
lessons.goal: Name and describe a conflict: Es gibt Streit wegen …; Mich stört, dass …; Es nervt mich, wenn …; name the feeling and say what you want.

grammar.topic: Describing a conflict: complaint chunks with dass and wenn
grammar.point: A complaint opener plus dass or wenn sends the verb to the end: Mich stört, dass die Küche voll ist. Es nervt mich, wenn du nachts kochst. Stören takes the accusative (mich). Describe the problem in four steps: what, since when, how you feel, what you want. No new grammar: you use dass, wenn and seitdem as you learned them.
grammar.oneLine: Mich stört, dass die Küche nachts voll ist.

mistake.wrong: Es stört mich, wenn du kochst nachts.
mistake.right: Es stört mich, wenn du nachts kochst.
mistake.why: After wenn the verb goes to the very end of the clause, so nachts has to stand before kochst.

terms.meaning: the case of the thing or person that is directly affected: mich, den Lärm
a sentence that says what bothers you

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ich ärgere mich' to describing a whole conflict
cards.body: It is February and the WG kitchen has turned into a battlefield. You can already say that something annoys you. Today you learn to describe a whole conflict: what happens, since when, how you feel and what you want. That is where every good talk begins.
steps: You already know: Ich ärgere mich über das Geschirr. One feeling about one thing, and dass- and wenn-clauses with the verb at the end.
New today: the words for a conflict and a way to describe it: what, since when, how you feel, what you want.
By the end you can: say what bothers you, name the feeling and describe a whole conflict in four steps.

examples.de: Ich ärgere mich über das Geschirr.
examples.en: I am annoyed about the dishes.
examples.why: You know this already: one feeling about one thing.

examples.de: Seitdem Anna packt und Leon nachts kocht, gibt es ständig Streit.
examples.en: Since Anna has been packing and Leon has been cooking at night, there is constant quarrelling.
examples.why: New today: a whole conflict in one sentence, with a time clause.

cards.more: Think of a conflict as a messy kitchen. If you only shout 'Chaos!', nobody knows where to start. If you say what you see, since when it has been like this and how you feel, the mess turns into a short list of small jobs. Today you build that list in German. You already own most tools: dass, wenn and seitdem. The next cards add the words for the quarrel and the feelings, step by step.

cards.title: The WG chat at half past twelve
cards.body: Read the group chat from the WG. Four people, four problems: noise at night, a full kitchen, boxes in the hall and no quiet for studying. Do not worry about every word. Find the sentences that complain and see how many use dass, wenn or seitdem.
cards.lead: Before any grammar comes the situation. This is the group chat late in February, when Anna is packing and Leon is practising recipes. Read it once and underline every complaint. The next cards take them apart.
steps: Mira: Es ist schon halb eins, und in der Küche klappert es wieder!
Leon: Ich übe nur ein Rezept für den Kochkurs. Morgen ist doch Donnerstag.
Mira: Seitdem du den Kochkurs machst, ist die Küche jeden Abend voll.
Ben: Und im Flur stehen Annas Kisten. Ich bin gestern fast über eine Kiste gefallen.
Anna: Ich packe doch nur! Im März bin ich weg.
Mira: Und der Putzplan? Das Geschirr steht seit Montag da.
Leon: Mira, du hast auch schon lange nicht mehr geputzt.
Mira: Ich brauche abends Ruhe, ich muss für die Bachelorarbeit lesen!

examples.de: Seitdem du den Kochkurs machst, ist die Küche jeden Abend voll.
examples.en: Since you have been doing the cooking course, the kitchen is full every evening.

examples.de: Ich bin gestern fast über eine Kiste gefallen.
examples.en: Yesterday I almost fell over a box.

examples.de: Ich brauche abends Ruhe!
examples.en: I need quiet in the evenings!

deeper.text: A chat drops words: no subject, no verb, just the feeling. Schon wieder Chaos in der Küche! is a complete message in a group chat. Friends write like this all the time. For a serious talk at the table, however, use full sentences, because short ones can sound like an attack.

example.de: Schon wieder Chaos in der Küche!
example.en: Chaos in the kitchen again!

cards.more: Imagine standing in the doorway of the kitchen at half past twelve and listening to four people at once. Mira is tired, Leon is busy, Ben nearly hurt himself and Anna feels guilty. Each of them says one short thing. Together the messages draw a picture of the problem. Your job in this card is only to see the picture. Later you will learn how to say your own part of it calmly.

cards.title: What disturbs me: four ways to start
cards.body: Four chunks start a complaint. Mich stört, dass … names a fact. Es nervt mich, wenn … names something that happens again and again. Ich ärgere mich darüber, dass … adds the feeling. Ich finde es nicht in Ordnung, dass … is the most serious. After dass or wenn the verb goes to the end.
cards.lead: Now you take the complaints from the chat and learn four fixed ways to say them. They all work the same: a short opener, a comma, then dass or wenn and the verb at the end.

examples.de: Mich stört, dass die Küche nachts voll ist.
examples.en: It bothers me that the kitchen is full at night.

examples.de: Es nervt mich, wenn du nachts kochst.
examples.en: It annoys me when you cook at night.

examples.de: Ich finde es nicht in Ordnung, dass die Kisten im Flur stehen.
examples.en: I do not think it is okay that the boxes are standing in the hall.

examples.de: Ich ärgere mich darüber, dass niemand abwäscht.
examples.en: I am annoyed that nobody washes up.

deeper.text: Stören takes the accusative, because the person is the one who is disturbed. Starting with Mich puts the person in first place and sounds a bit stronger than Es stört mich, dass …; both are correct. The thing that disturbs can also be a noun: Mich stört der Lärm, dich nicht?

example.de: Mich stört der Lärm, dich nicht?
example.en: The noise bothers me, does it not bother you?

cards.more: Imagine the opener as a polite knock on a door. First you knock: Mich stört, … or Es nervt mich, … Then you say what is behind the door. If it is a fact, you open with dass. If it happens again and again, you open with wenn. Whatever follows the comma, the verb walks to the back of the room. Mira never says that Leon is bad. She says what happens and how it hits her.

rows: Mich stört, dass die Küche nachts voll ist.
Es nervt mich, wenn du nachts kochst.
Ich ärgere mich darüber, dass niemand abwäscht.
Ich finde es nicht in Ordnung, dass …
Ich finde es nicht in Ordnung, dass die Kisten im Flur stehen.

cards.title: Conflict words: Streit, Vorwurf, Auseinandersetzung
cards.body: A conflict has several names. Der Streit is the everyday quarrel. Der Vorwurf is a reproach, and you reproach someone with vorwerfen. Die Meinungsverschiedenheit is a mild disagreement. Die Auseinandersetzung is longer and more serious than a quarrel. Nouns and verbs belong together, so learn them in pairs.
cards.lead: A complaint can turn into a quarrel, and German has different words for how big it is. This card puts the nouns and the verbs of a conflict in families, from small to serious.

examples.de: Mira wirft Leon vor, dass er nachts kocht.
examples.en: Mira reproaches Leon for cooking at night.

examples.de: Das war kein Streit, nur eine Meinungsverschiedenheit.
examples.en: That was not a quarrel, only a disagreement.

examples.de: Nach der Auseinandersetzung sprachen sie zwei Tage nicht miteinander.
examples.en: After the argument they did not speak to each other for two days.

deeper.text: German has a colourful chunk for a quarrel: sich in die Haare kriegen, literally to get into each other's hair. It is colloquial and slightly funny, so use it with friends and not in a formal talk. Friends who always quarrel are Leute, die sich ständig in die Haare kriegen.

example.de: Die beiden kriegen sich ständig in die Haare.
example.en: The two of them are constantly at each other's throats.

cards.more: Picture a staircase with three steps. On the lowest step there is the Meinungsverschiedenheit: two people simply think differently and nobody shouts. The middle step is the Streit: voices are loud. The top step is the Auseinandersetzung: it goes on for days and needs a serious talk. The Vorwurf is a stone people throw while they climb: Du hast schon wieder nicht geputzt! Knowing the step helps you say how big the problem really is.

rows: reproach, to reproach someone for something

cards.title: Feelings in a conflict
cards.body: Under every quarrel there is a feeling. Ich bin enttäuscht means you hoped for more. Verletzt means someone hurt you. Sauer is everyday German for angry, but milder than wütend. Unfair behandelt is a whole chunk: treated unfairly. Name the feeling and you describe the conflict more honestly.
cards.lead: Complaints are about things, but feelings are about you. This card gives you four words for how a conflict feels, so that you can say more than just Ich bin genervt.

examples.de: Ich bin enttäuscht, dass ihr den Putzplan vergessen habt.
examples.en: I am disappointed that you all forgot the cleaning rota.

examples.de: Anna ist verletzt, weil die anderen über ihre Kisten schimpfen.
examples.en: Anna is hurt because the others are grumbling about her boxes.

examples.de: Ich bin sauer, weil niemand abgewaschen hat.
examples.en: I am cross because nobody has washed up.

deeper.text: Sauer literally means sour, and in everyday speech it means angry. It is milder and more colloquial than wütend: a friend who is sauer is cross, not furious. You say sauer auf jemanden sein, with auf and the accusative. In a formal letter prefer verärgert or wütend.

example.de: Bist du sauer auf mich?
example.en: Are you cross with me?

cards.more: Think of feelings as the weather behind the quarrel. Enttäuscht is a grey sky: I hoped for something and it did not happen. Verletzt is a sharp wind: something you said or did hurt me. Sauer is a short rain shower: loud, quick, and often gone by dinner. When you only say 'Ich bin genervt', everybody feels the same weather. When you pick the exact word, the other person understands what is really going on.

rows: you feel it is not fair

cards.title: Typical WG conflicts
cards.body: Almost every shared flat quarrels about the same five things: Lärm, Ordnung, Putzen, Besuch and Geld. Each topic has its own chunk. Lärm and the Ruhezeit, Unordnung in the hall, who has to clean, friends who stay too long, and who pays for the shared things. Learn the topics and you can name the problem fast.
cards.lead: Shared flats have a few classic fights. Here are the five topics with the sentences you will need, so that in a real WG you recognise the problem and can name it.

examples.de: Nach 22 Uhr gilt in unserem Haus die Ruhezeit.
examples.en: After ten in the evening the quiet hours apply in our house.

examples.de: Ich finde es unordentlich, wenn Schuhe im Flur liegen.
examples.en: I find it untidy when shoes lie in the hall.

examples.de: Wir zahlen jeden Monat zehn Euro in die WG-Kasse.
examples.en: Every month we pay ten euros into the shared kitty.

deeper.text: In many German shared flats there are two typical things: the WG-Kasse, a shared kitty for toilet paper, washing-up liquid and similar items, and the Putzplan, a list that says who cleans what in which week. It is a tendency, not a law, but a flat without a plan often ends up with exactly the quarrels of this chapter.

example.de: Wer ist diese Woche mit dem Putzen dran?
example.en: Whose turn is it to clean this week?

cards.more: Imagine a shared flat as a small village with five rules. The noise rule says when it must be quiet. The order rule says where shoes and boxes belong. The cleaning rule says whose turn it is. The guest rule says how long friends may stay. The money rule says who pays for what. Most WG fights are one of these rules that nobody agreed on out loud. That is why the next lesson ends with an agreement.

rows: music or cooking late at night

cards.title: Describe a conflict in four steps
cards.body: A clear description has four steps. What happens? Since when? How do you feel? What do you want? Use a plain fact, a time clause with seitdem or immer wenn, a feeling word and a wish with ich möchte. Mira: Die Küche ist nachts voll. Seitdem Leon kocht, ist es jeden Abend so. Ich bin genervt. Ich möchte abends Ruhe.
cards.lead: Now you put everything together. Four small steps turn a quarrel into a clear message, and each step uses something you have just learned.
steps: 1. What happens? Die Küche ist nachts voll.
2. Since when? Seitdem Leon den Kochkurs macht, ist es jeden Abend so.
3. How do I feel? Ich bin genervt.
4. What do I want? Ich möchte abends Ruhe haben.

examples.de: Die Küche ist nachts voll.
examples.en: The kitchen is full at night.

examples.de: Seitdem Leon den Kochkurs macht, ist es jeden Abend so.
examples.en: Since Leon has been doing the cooking course, it has been like this every evening.

examples.de: Ich bin genervt, und ich möchte abends Ruhe haben.
examples.en: I am annoyed and I would like quiet in the evenings.

deeper.text: Your description gets stronger if you describe the problem and not the person. Compare Du bist unordentlich with Die Küche ist unordentlich. The first attacks someone, the second describes a fact that both of you can look at. The next lesson builds on this: it turns complaints into Ich-Botschaften.

example.de: Die Küche ist unordentlich, und ich ärgere mich darüber.
example.en: The kitchen is untidy and I am annoyed about it.

cards.more: Think of the four steps as four boxes on a form. Box one: what. Box two: since when. Box three: how I feel. Box four: what I want. If you leave a box empty, the other person has to guess. If you fill all four, they can answer straight away. Try it with a small problem first, like the dishes, and then you will manage with bigger ones like the nightly cooking.

lessons.title: Lass uns darüber reden: ein Konfliktgespräch führen
lessons.goal: Hold a conflict talk and find a compromise: Ich fühle mich …, wenn …; Wie wäre es, wenn …?; Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …?; apologise and make up.

grammar.topic: Conflict talk: Ich-Botschaften and suggestions with dass and wenn
grammar.point: Say how you feel with Ich + feeling + wenn-clause: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist. Suggest a compromise with Wie wäre es, wenn …? Ich schlage vor, dass … Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …? The verb goes to the end of every wenn- and dass-clause. No new grammar: you use wenn, dass and wäre as you know them.
grammar.oneLine: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist.

mistake.wrong: Ich schlage vor, dass wir machen einen Putzplan.
mistake.right: Ich schlage vor, dass wir einen Putzplan machen.
mistake.why: After dass the verb goes to the very end of the clause, behind the object.

terms.meaning: a sentence that says how you feel instead of blaming the other person
a solution where both sides give a little

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Mich stört, dass …' to a talk that solves the problem
cards.body: Last time you learned to say what bothers you. But a complaint alone does not clean the kitchen. Tonight the WG sits at the table to talk. Today you learn to say how you feel without attacking anyone and to suggest a solution that everybody can accept.
steps: You already know: Mich stört, dass die Küche nie sauber ist. A complaint with dass and the verb at the end.
New today: Ich-Botschaften, a calm order for the talk, and sentences that suggest a compromise or say sorry.
By the end you can: lead a conflict talk, suggest a compromise, apologise and agree on rules.

examples.de: Mich stört, dass die Küche nie sauber ist.
examples.en: It bothers me that the kitchen is never clean.
examples.why: You know this already: a complaint about a fact.

examples.de: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist.
examples.en: I feel stressed when the kitchen is full at night.
examples.why: New today: the same fact, told as your own feeling.

examples.de: Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass Leon bis 22 Uhr kocht?
examples.en: Can we agree that Leon cooks until 10 pm?
examples.why: New today: a question that asks for a deal.

cards.more: Imagine a bridge. On one side stands the complaint, on the other side a solution. A complaint alone is like shouting across the river. A talk is the bridge: you say how you feel, you listen to the other person, you suggest something and you shake hands. You already know the planks, dass and wenn, from the last lesson. In the next cards you learn the order in which to lay them, step by step.

cards.title: The kitchen-table talk
cards.body: Read the whole talk once. Mira starts calmly, Leon defends himself, Ben mediates and Anna says sorry. Look at how Mira speaks about herself and not about Leon: Ich fühle mich … Then watch how the others suggest a solution.
cards.lead: Tonight the WG finally talks at the kitchen table. This card shows the whole conversation, so you can see how the pieces of the next cards fit together before we take them apart.
steps: Mira: Ich möchte mit euch reden. Das geht so nicht weiter.
Ben: Ja, lass uns mal in Ruhe reden. Mira, fang du an.
Mira: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist. Ich muss für die Bachelorarbeit lernen.
Leon: Das sehe ich anders. Ich koche doch nicht laut. Ich übe nur für den Kurs.
Ben: Leon, lass Mira bitte ausreden.
Mira: Ich möchte nur sagen: Ich bin müde, und ich brauche abends Ruhe.
Leon: Ich verstehe. Aber ich habe nur abends Zeit, tagsüber bin ich an der Uni.
Ben: Wie wäre es, wenn Leon bis 22 Uhr kocht?
Leon: Das geht. Dann koche ich eben früher. Können wir uns darauf einigen?
Anna: Und ich räume die Kisten bis Freitag in mein Zimmer. Es tut mir leid, dass sie im Flur stehen.
Mira: Danke, Anna. Und wir machen einen neuen Putzplan.
Ben: Gut, dann haben wir eine Lösung.

examples.de: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist.
examples.en: I feel stressed when the kitchen is full at night.

examples.de: Ich habe nur abends Zeit, tagsüber bin ich an der Uni.
examples.en: I only have time in the evening, during the day I am at university.

examples.de: Wie wäre es, wenn Leon bis 22 Uhr kocht?
examples.en: How about Leon cooking until 10 pm?

deeper.text: Ben does not take a side: he schlichtet, he settles the quarrel. A neutral person who helps two sides to talk is a Schlichter or a Schlichterin. His job is to keep the talk calm and to ask for suggestions, not to decide. Such a helper often finds the compromise faster than the two people who are angry.

example.de: Ben schlichtet den Streit zwischen Mira und Leon.
example.en: Ben settles the quarrel between Mira and Leon.

cards.more: Think of the talk as a small play with four roles. Mira is the one who opens. Leon is the one who explains. Ben is the referee who keeps both sides calm. Anna is the one who admits her own part. Nobody shouts and nobody leaves the room. At the end there is a list of rules that everyone can live with. Keep this play in your mind: the next cards are its scenes.

cards.title: Ich-Botschaft instead of Du-Vorwurf
cards.body: A Du-Vorwurf attacks: Du machst immer Chaos! The other person defends himself at once. An Ich-Botschaft says how you feel: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist. The pattern is Ich + feeling + wenn + what happens, with the verb at the end of the wenn-clause.
cards.lead: In the talk Mira did not say 'You are the problem'. She said how she feels. This card shows the trick and gives you a pattern to copy for your own complaints.

examples.de: Ich bin traurig, wenn niemand mir zuhört.
examples.en: I am sad when nobody listens to me.

examples.de: Ich ärgere mich, wenn Sachen im Flur liegen.
examples.en: I get annoyed when things are lying in the hall.

examples.de: Ich bin müde, wenn es nachts laut ist.
examples.en: I am tired when it is loud at night.

deeper.text: Ich-Botschaften come from psychology and communication training. The idea is simple: the other person can argue with You are …, but cannot argue with how you feel. Germans use them in the family, at work and in a WG. You can also say it with fühlen: Ich fühle mich nicht gehört, wenn du mich unterbrichst.

example.de: Ich fühle mich nicht gehört, wenn du mich unterbrichst.
example.en: I do not feel heard when you interrupt me.

cards.more: Think of two doors. The Du-Vorwurf is a door that slams: 'You always …!' The other person pushes back at once. The Ich-Botschaft is a door that opens a little: 'I feel …, when …'. There is nothing to push against, so the other person listens. The recipe has three ingredients: I, a feeling, and what happens. Do not add the word immer, because 'always' starts the quarrel again.

rows: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist.
Ich bin traurig, wenn niemand mir zuhört.
Ich ärgere mich, wenn Sachen im Flur liegen.

cards.title: The steps of a conflict talk
cards.body: A good talk has an order. Start calmly. Describe what happens. Say how you feel. Listen and let the other person finish. Then make a suggestion and agree on it. If you skip a step, the talk often turns into a quarrel again. Mira follows these steps almost exactly.
cards.lead: Mira's talk worked because it followed an order. Here are the six steps with a German chunk for each, so you can use the same order in your own conversations.
steps: 1. Start calmly: Lass uns mal in Ruhe reden.
2. Describe: Seitdem Leon den Kurs macht, ist die Küche abends voll.
3. Say your feeling: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn …
4. Listen: Lass mich bitte ausreden! / Das sehe ich anders.
5. Suggest: Wie wäre es, wenn …?
6. Agree: Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …?

examples.de: Lass uns mal in Ruhe reden.
examples.en: Let us talk calmly for a moment.

examples.de: Lass mich bitte ausreden!
examples.en: Please let me finish!

examples.de: Das sehe ich anders, aber ich verstehe dich.
examples.en: I see that differently, but I understand you.

deeper.text: Jemanden ausreden lassen is an important politeness rule in German talks: you wait until the other person has finished. Interrupting is often felt as rude, especially in a serious conversation. If someone interrupts you, say Lass mich bitte ausreden! If you interrupt by accident, say Entschuldigung, sprich bitte weiter.

example.de: Entschuldigung, sprich bitte weiter.
example.en: Sorry, please go on.

cards.more: Think of the six steps as a staircase down from a loud room to a quiet one. At the top everybody is tense. Step by step you go down: calm start, facts, feelings, listening, a suggestion, an agreement. If someone jumps down two steps at once, for example straight to the suggestion, the other person feels nobody listened. Take the steps in order and the stairs are safe, even when you are angry.

cards.title: Suggesting a compromise
cards.body: Four chunks suggest a compromise. Wie wäre es, wenn …? is soft, with the wish form wäre. Ich schlage vor, dass … is clear. Was hältst du davon, wenn …? asks for an opinion. Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …? asks for the deal. All four end with a clause with the verb at the end.
cards.lead: After the feelings comes the solution. Here are four ways to suggest a compromise, from very soft to a clear request for agreement. Each one opens a dass- or wenn-clause.

examples.de: Ich schlage vor, dass wir einen neuen Putzplan machen.
examples.en: I suggest that we make a new cleaning rota.

examples.de: Was hältst du davon, wenn Anna die Kisten bis Freitag in ihr Zimmer stellt?
examples.en: What do you think of Anna putting the boxes in her room by Friday?

examples.de: Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass wir nach 22 Uhr leise sind?
examples.en: Can we agree that we are quiet after 10 pm?

deeper.text: In German the word Kompromiss is positive: in politics, in a family and in a WG people are proud of a good compromise. But there is also the fauler Kompromiss, a lazy compromise where nobody gets what they wanted and everybody is a little unhappy. Note the ending: ein fauler Kompromiss.

example.de: Das ist ein fauler Kompromiss, und keiner ist zufrieden.
example.en: That is a lazy compromise and nobody is satisfied.

cards.more: Think of a compromise as cutting a cake. Wie wäre es, wenn …? is the soft knife: you only show what is possible. Ich schlage vor, dass … is the clear cut. Was hältst du davon, wenn …? hands the knife to the other person. Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …? is the moment where both agree on the pieces. Use the soft knife first, and only reach for the clear one when the talk is calm.

rows: Wie wäre es, wenn Leon bis 22 Uhr kocht?
Ich schlage vor, dass wir einen neuen Putzplan machen.
Was hältst du davon, wenn wir Ruhezeiten haben?
Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass …?
Können wir uns darauf einigen, dass wir leise sind?

cards.title: Saying sorry and making up
cards.body: A talk often ends with sorry and a handshake. Es tut mir leid, dass … says what you regret. Das war nicht so gemeint explains that you did not want to hurt someone. Schon gut accepts the apology. Wir haben uns versöhnt says that the quarrel is over. Sich versöhnen is a reflexive verb, so it needs sich.
cards.lead: Every conflict talk needs a way out. This card gives you the sentences for apologising, for accepting an apology and for saying that you are friends again.

examples.de: Es tut mir leid, dass die Kisten im Flur stehen.
examples.en: I am sorry that the boxes are standing in the hall.

examples.de: Das war nicht so gemeint.
examples.en: I did not mean it like that.

examples.de: Mira und Leon haben sich versöhnt.
examples.en: Mira and Leon have made up.

deeper.text: Sich versöhnen is a real reconciliation after a serious quarrel. Sich vertragen is lighter and more colloquial: it means to get along again, and you often hear it about children: Die Kinder haben sich wieder vertragen. Between adults a small quarrel ends with Schon gut, wir vertragen uns wieder.

example.de: Die Kinder haben sich wieder vertragen.
example.en: The children are getting along again.

cards.more: Think of an apology as three small pieces. First you say what you are sorry about: Es tut mir leid, dass … Then you say you did not mean it: Das war nicht so gemeint. The other person answers with Schon gut when they accept. Only then can you say Wir haben uns versöhnt. If you jump to the last piece, it sounds as if nothing happened. If you skip the first piece, the sorry sounds empty.

rows: You did not want to hurt

cards.title: The result: the new WG rules
cards.body: At the end of the talk the WG has an Abmachung, an agreement. It has three rules: Leon cooks until 22 Uhr, there is a new Putzplan, and Anna moves the boxes into her room by Friday. A good agreement is short, clear and has times. Everyone has to stick to it: sich an etwas halten.
cards.lead: A conflict talk is only worth something if it ends with clear rules. Here are the rules of the WG, and the chunk that you need to say that you will keep to them.
steps: Leon kocht bis 22 Uhr.
Es gibt einen neuen Putzplan: jede Woche ist eine andere Person dran.
Anna räumt die Kisten bis Freitag in ihr Zimmer.
Nach 22 Uhr ist Ruhezeit.

examples.de: Leon kocht nur noch bis 22 Uhr.
examples.en: Leon only cooks until 10 pm now.

examples.de: Anna räumt die Kisten bis Freitag in ihr Zimmer.
examples.en: Anna puts the boxes in her room by Friday.

examples.de: Wir halten uns alle an die Abmachung.
examples.en: We all stick to the agreement.

deeper.text: Many shared flats write the agreement down and hang it on the fridge, because a rule on paper is harder to forget. It is not a legal contract, only a promise between friends. If somebody breaks it, you do not shout, you go back to the table and talk again.

example.de: Wir hängen die Abmachung an den Kühlschrank.
example.en: We hang the agreement on the fridge.

cards.more: Think of the agreement as a small map for the next weeks. It shows three roads: when Leon cooks, how the cleaning works, and what happens to the boxes. Every road has a sign with a time: bis 22 Uhr, jede Woche, bis Freitag. A map without times is not much help, because 'later' can mean tomorrow or never. If you stick to the map, nobody gets lost in the kitchen again.

lessons.title: Das ist doch nicht so schlimm: Modalpartikeln und Intonation
lessons.goal: Understand and use modal particles with the right melody: doch, ja, mal, denn, eigentlich, halt/eben.

grammar.topic: Modal particles: doch, ja, mal, denn, eigentlich, halt/eben
grammar.point: Modal particles are small unstressed words inside the sentence that add a feeling. Doch reminds or pushes (Komm doch mit!), ja shows shared knowledge or surprise (Das ist ja toll!), mal softens a request (Kannst du mal helfen?), denn shows interest in a question (Was ist denn los?), eigentlich means by the way, halt and eben mean that is how it is. They stand after the verb and the pronouns, never at position 1. The melody carries the feeling.
grammar.oneLine: Komm doch mit! Was ist denn los?

mistake.why: A modal particle never stands at position 1. It stands after the verb (and pronouns).

terms.meaning: a small word like doch or mal that adds a feeling to the sentence
the word you say louder and higher in a sentence

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Doch!' to doch in the middle of a sentence
cards.body: After the talk the WG laughs and relaxes, and suddenly everybody sounds different: Komm doch mit! Das ist doch nicht so schlimm. Small words like doch, ja or mal sit inside the sentence. They do not change the facts, only the feeling. Today you learn to hear them and to use them.
steps: You already know: Hast du keine Zeit? – Doch! Doch is the answer that says yes to a negative question.
New today: doch, ja, mal, denn, eigentlich and halt/eben inside a sentence, and how the melody carries the feeling.
By the end you can: understand the feeling of these words and use two or three of them yourself.

examples.de: Hast du keine Zeit?
examples.en: Do you not have time?
examples.why: You know this already: doch as the answer to a no-question.

examples.de: Doch!
examples.en: Yes, I do!
examples.why: You know this already: doch contradicts a negative question.

examples.de: Komm doch mit!
examples.en: Come along!
examples.why: New today: doch in the middle of the sentence, as a friendly push.

examples.de: Das ist doch nicht so schlimm.
examples.en: It is not that bad, after all.
examples.why: New today: doch as a gentle reminder.

cards.more: Imagine a sentence as a plain white shirt. Modal particles are small buttons, scarves and badges: the shirt stays the same, but the look changes. Komm mit! is the plain shirt. Komm doch mit! has a friendly scarf. Natives wear these little words all day in speech, and a learner who never uses them sounds correct but a bit stiff. You will meet six of them, one card at a time.

cards.title: Same sentence, different feeling
cards.body: A modal particle is a small word inside the sentence that adds a feeling: interest, surprise, friendliness or impatience. Compare Was ist los? with Was ist denn los? The second sounds interested and kind. Komm her. can sound like an order, Komm mal her. is friendlier. The facts stay the same.
cards.lead: Before we sort the particles, listen for the difference they make. This card shows three pairs of sentences: first without a particle, then with one, so you can feel what the little word does.

examples.de: Was ist denn los?
examples.en: What is going on?

examples.de: Komm mal her.
examples.en: Come over here for a moment.

examples.de: Das ist ja toll!
examples.en: That is great!

deeper.text: Written German uses fewer particles than speech. In a formal letter or a news article you will hardly find them, but in chats, dialogues and everyday talk they appear in almost every second sentence. That is why you learn them by ear: read a particle sentence aloud and listen for the mood.

example.de: Wie geht es dir denn?
example.en: And how are you, then?

cards.more: Think of a sentence with a particle like a photo with a filter. Without the filter the picture is neutral: Was ist los? just asks for information. With denn the picture gets warm: I am interested and I care. With ja a surprised, happy colour comes in. You do not learn new facts, you learn the mood of the picture. If you read a German dialogue, ask yourself in every line what mood the little word adds.

cards.title: doch and ja
cards.body: Doch in the middle of a sentence reminds the listener of something he knows or gives a friendly push: Das weißt du doch! Setz dich doch! Ja means that something is known to everybody or that you are surprised: Du weißt ja, dass ich abends lerne. Das ist ja toll! Both stand after the verb and are not stressed.
cards.lead: Now the first two particles in detail. Doch and ja both point to something you and the listener already know, but they sound different: doch reminds or pushes, ja shares or is surprised.

examples.de: Das weißt du doch!
examples.en: But you know that!

examples.de: Setz dich doch!
examples.en: Do sit down!

examples.de: Du weißt ja, dass ich abends lerne.
examples.en: You know, of course, that I study in the evening.

examples.de: Das ist ja toll!
examples.en: That is great!

deeper.text: If you stress doch, it changes its meaning: it means after all or really, and it often contradicts what somebody expected. Er ist DOCH gekommen. means He came after all. Compare this with the unstressed doch in Das weißt du doch!, which is a reminder. The stress turns the little word into a big one.

example.de: Er ist DOCH gekommen.
example.en: He came after all.

cards.more: Imagine you and your friend share a notebook of things you both know. When you say doch, you tap the notebook: 'Look, it is written there, you know this.' When you say ja, you smile and show a page: 'As you know …' or 'Wow, look at this!' Both little words say 'we share this knowledge'. The difference is the mood: doch is a gentle push, ja is a shared smile or surprise.

rows: Das weißt du doch! Setz dich doch!
Du weißt ja, … Das ist ja toll!

cards.title: mal and denn
cards.body: Mal makes a request softer. Kannst du mal helfen? sounds friendlier than Kannst du helfen? It often means just or for a moment, even if the action is not short. Denn appears in questions and shows interest or surprise: Wo warst du denn? Both stand after the verb and the pronoun.
cards.lead: Two particles for talking to people: mal for polite requests and denn for questions that show that you care. Together they make your German sound much more natural and friendly.

examples.de: Kannst du mal helfen?
examples.en: Can you help for a moment?

examples.de: Hör mal zu!
examples.en: Listen for a moment!

examples.de: Wo warst du denn?
examples.en: Where were you, then?

deeper.text: Komm mal her is friendly, but Komm her can sound like an order, like a teacher calling a child. With mal the same request becomes an invitation. The tone also decides: a stern Komm mal HER! with a sharp voice can sound strict again. The particle only helps if the melody agrees with it.

example.de: Komm mal her, ich zeige dir etwas.
example.en: Come here for a moment, I will show you something.

cards.more: Think of mal as a soft cushion under your request. Without it, the request lands hard: Hilf mir! With it, the same request lands softly: Hilf mir mal! The cushion says 'it is only a small thing'. Denn is a curious face in a question: Wo warst du denn? means 'I really want to know'. A question without denn is only a question; with denn it shows that you are interested in the answer.

rows: Kannst du mal helfen? Hör mal zu!
shows interest or surprise in a question
Wo warst du denn? Was ist denn los?

cards.title: eigentlich, halt and eben
cards.body: Eigentlich means by the way or actually: Wie heißt du eigentlich? It lightly changes the topic. Halt and eben both mean that is just how it is and that nobody can change it: Das ist halt so. Dann eben nicht. They sound resigned or calm. Say them with a shrug.
cards.lead: The last group is a bit more difficult, because the English translation is not exact. These three particles say: by the way, and that is just how it is. Learn them as little attitude words.

examples.de: Wie heißt du eigentlich?
examples.en: By the way, what is your name?

examples.de: Das ist halt so.
examples.en: That is just how it is.

examples.de: Dann gehen wir eben ohne dich.
examples.en: Then we simply go without you.

deeper.text: Halt is typical for the South and for Austria, eben is more common in the North. This is a tendency, not a rule, and everybody understands both. If you hear Das ist halt so in Wien and Das ist eben so in Hamburg, they mean the same thing. As a learner you may choose one and use it.

example.de: Dann eben nicht.
example.en: Then not, that's fine.

cards.more: Think of halt and eben as a shrug. 'Das ist halt so' means: this is how things are and there is no use in fighting it. 'Dann eben nicht' means: all right, if you do not want to, then we will not. Eigentlich is a small door to a new topic: you were talking about the weather, and now you ask 'Wie heißt du eigentlich?' because you suddenly think of it. Eigentlich often shows that the question is a bit unplanned.

rows: that is how it is (South, Austria)

cards.title: Where the particle goes
cards.body: Particles stand inside the sentence: after the verb and after pronouns, before the new or important information. Das ist ja SUPER. Du kannst doch heute mitkommen. They never stand at position 1, so Doch komm mit! is wrong, and Komm doch mit! is right. Particles are also not stressed.
cards.lead: Knowing the word is half the work. This card shows the place: always after the verb and the pronouns, and before the part of the sentence you want to emphasise.
steps: Find the verb: kannst, ist, haben.
Put the pronouns next: du, wir, mir.
Insert the particle: doch, ja, mal.
Then the new or important information: heute, super, das Salz.

examples.de: Du kannst doch heute mitkommen.
examples.en: You can come along today, after all.

examples.de: Wir haben ja schon gegessen.
examples.en: We have already eaten, as you know.

examples.de: Gibst du mir mal das Salz?
examples.en: Will you pass me the salt?

deeper.text: Particles can also be combined. The most common pair is doch mal, in this order: Komm doch mal mit! sounds even friendlier than Komm doch mit! because the push of doch and the softness of mal work together. Do not mix up the order: Komm mal doch mit! is unusual.

example.de: Komm doch mal mit!
example.en: Do come along!

cards.more: Imagine the sentence as a train: the verb is the engine, and the pronouns are the first carriages. The particle gets a seat right behind them. After the particle come the new and important carriages, the ones you want the listener to look at. That is why the particle never stands at the front: the front of the train is for the engine. If you want to place a particle, find the verb and the pronouns, and put the particle behind them.

cards.title: Intonation: the melody does the work
cards.body: The particle itself is not stressed. The stress goes to the word that follows, and the melody carries the feeling. Das ist ja SUPER with a rising voice means happy surprise. Das ist doch nicht so schlimm said gently calms someone. The same words with a sharp, falling voice sound impatient. Replay the WG talk and listen to it.
cards.lead: Particles live in the melody. This last card shows how the voice changes the feeling and replays the WG talk with particles, so you can read it aloud and hear the difference.
steps: Ben: Was ist denn los, Mira?
Mira: Ich fühle mich gestresst, wenn die Küche nachts voll ist. Das weißt du doch, Leon.
Leon: Ich koche ja nicht laut. Ich übe doch nur für den Kurs.
Ben: Hör mal zu, Leon. Lass Mira doch ausreden.
Leon: Dann koche ich eben früher.
Anna: Das ist doch nicht so schlimm. Wir finden schon eine Lösung.
Mira: Na ja, das ist halt so in einer WG. Man muss reden.

examples.de: Das ist doch nicht so schlimm.
examples.en: It is not that bad, after all.

examples.de: Lass Mira doch ausreden.
examples.en: Do let Mira finish.

examples.de: Ich übe doch nur für den Kurs.
examples.en: But I am only practising for the course.

deeper.text: Particles are hard to translate because English uses the tone of voice, words like just, after all, anyway, or nothing at all. German puts the feeling into a small word, English into the melody. So do not look for a one-to-one translation: look at what the speaker feels and say it in your own words.

example.de: Du bist ja ganz nass!
example.en: Oh, you are all wet!

cards.more: Think of the particle as a quiet guest at a loud party. The guest sits down and does not say a thing, but the mood of the party changes. The loud guest is the stressed word after the particle. Your voice does the rest: going up shows surprise or interest, going down shows impatience or a shrug. If you read the replay below aloud, first with a flat voice and then with feeling, you will hear how much the voice carries.

drills.prompt: Was ist ___ los?
drills.hint: Which particle makes a question sound interested?
drills.explanation: Was ist denn los?

drills.prompt: Kannst du mir ___ helfen? (softens the request)

lessons.title: Darf ich vorstellen? Ein Paar erzählt
lessons.goal: Introduce a couple, tell the stages of a relationship and talk about two famous couples.

grammar.topic: Introducing a couple (use of Plusquamperfekt, nachdem and seit/seitdem)
grammar.point: No new grammar. You introduce a couple with a fixed frame and tell the earlier events in Plusquamperfekt with nachdem; seit/seitdem links the past to today. Zusammen and verheiratet stand last, after the time phrase.
grammar.oneLine: Nachdem sie sich auf einer WG-Party kennengelernt hatten, waren sie bald ein Paar.

mistake.wrong: Sie sind zusammen seit fünf Jahren.
mistake.right: Sie sind seit fünf Jahren zusammen.
mistake.why: Zusammen stands at the end like a separable prefix, and the time phrase comes before it.

terms.meaning: one step of a relationship, from meeting to marriage (die Phase)
das Paar: two people who belong together; das Ehepaar: a married couple

cards.title: Before we start: from 'Ben ist Annas Mann' to a couple's whole story
cards.body: So far you can say who people are. Today you tell a couple's whole story: how they met, what came next and how long they have been together. You already know Plusquamperfekt, nachdem and seit. Today you put them to work.
steps: You already know: Ben und Anna sind verheiratet.
New today: Nachdem sie sich auf einer WG-Party kennengelernt hatten, waren sie bald ein Paar.
By the end: you can introduce a couple, name the stages of a relationship and tell the story of two famous couples.

examples.de: Ben und Anna sind verheiratet.
examples.en: Ben and Anna are married.
examples.why: You know this: a plain fact.

examples.de: Nachdem sie sich auf einer WG-Party kennengelernt hatten, waren sie bald ein Paar.
examples.en: After they had met at a flat party, they soon were a couple.
examples.why: New today: a whole story in one sentence. The first event is in Plusquamperfekt.

examples.de: Sie sind seit Jahren ein Paar.
examples.en: They have been a couple for years.
examples.why: seit + Dativ: it began in the past and still goes on.

cards.more: Think of a photo album. The first page has one photo with a short caption: Ben und Anna sind verheiratet. A real album tells more. It shows the party, the long talk, the first date and the move to a shared flat. Each picture needs a caption that says what came first and what came after. That is today's work: captions with hatten and waren for the earlier pictures, and nachdem or seitdem to link them.

cards.title: „Paare im Kiez“: Ben und Anna erzählen
cards.lead: The Viertel-hilft newsletter has a series about couples in the neighbourhood. Read how Ben and Anna tell their story, and watch how Plusquamperfekt and seitdem carry it.
cards.body: Mira asks the questions. Read the interview once for the story and once for the grammar. Sentences with hatten tell what happened first, the main clause tells what came next, and seitdem leads from the past into today.
steps: Mira: Wie habt ihr euch kennengelernt?
Ben: Auf einer WG-Party in Berlin. Nachdem wir uns lange unterhalten hatten, gab Anna mir ihre Nummer.
Mira: War es Liebe auf den ersten Blick?
Anna: Nein, eher auf den zweiten. Ben hatte den ganzen Abend in der Küche gestanden, und ich hatte ihn gar nicht gesehen.
Mira: Was habt ihr gemeinsam?
Ben: Wir kochen beide gern und gehen oft spazieren.
Anna: Unterschiede gibt es auch: Ben räumt sofort auf, und ich lasse meine Farben überall liegen.
Mira: Wie schafft ihr das Jahr, in dem Anna in Wien ist?
Ben: Wir führen eine Fernbeziehung. Seitdem wir das entschieden haben, sind wir ruhiger.

examples.de: Nachdem wir uns lange unterhalten hatten, gab Anna mir ihre Nummer.
examples.en: After we had talked for a long time, Anna gave me her number.
examples.why: The talk came first (Plusquamperfekt), the number came next (Präteritum).

examples.de: Ben hatte den ganzen Abend in der Küche gestanden.
examples.en: Ben had stood in the kitchen all evening.
examples.why: hatte + Partizip II at the end: a flashback.

examples.de: Seitdem wir das entschieden haben, sind wir ruhiger.
examples.en: Since we decided that, we have been calmer.
examples.why: The decision lies in the past, but being calm is true now: Perfekt, then Präsens.

deeper.text: Fernbeziehung is the usual word for a couple who live in different cities. If they meet only at the weekend, Germans say Wochenendbeziehung. Both words are feminine and you hear them in everyday talk, in magazines and at work. The verb that goes with them is führen: eine Fernbeziehung führen.

example.de: Viele Paare führen eine Wochenendbeziehung.
example.en: Many couples have a weekend relationship.

cards.more: Imagine the interview as a short film. First comes the flashback: the party, the long talk, Ben in the kitchen. These scenes are earlier, so they use hatte or war plus Partizip II. Then the film cuts to the next scene, the phone number, in Präteritum. Seitdem is the bridge back to today: the decision started in the past, but the calm is true now, so the main clause stands in Präsens. Three tenses, one story.

cards.title: Ein Paar vorstellen
cards.lead: After the interview you need a short frame you can reuse. These five questions let you introduce any couple in under a minute.
cards.body: Name the couple, say since when, tell how they met, then what they share and what is different. Zusammen and verheiratet stand at the end, like a separable prefix. The time phrase comes before them.

rows: Sie sind seit dreißig Jahren verheiratet.
Sie haben sich beim Studium kennengelernt.
Gemeinsam ist ihnen die Liebe zur Musik.
Er ist ruhig, und sie redet gern.

examples.de: Das sind meine Eltern.
examples.en: These are my parents.
examples.why: Role nouns like Eltern, Freunde or Nachbarn are fine for real people.

examples.de: Sie sind seit dreißig Jahren verheiratet.
examples.en: They have been married for thirty years.
examples.why: seit + Dativ plural: Jahren.

examples.de: Sie haben sich beim Studium kennengelernt.
examples.en: They met during their studies.
examples.why: sich kennenlernen is reflexive and takes haben.

examples.de: Gemeinsam ist ihnen die Liebe zur Musik.
examples.en: What they share is a love of music.
examples.why: A fixed frame: Gemeinsam ist ihnen …

deeper.text: Das Ehepaar is a married couple, das Paar is any two people who belong together. Watch the small word too: ein Paar with a capital P is a couple, ein paar with a small p means a few. You cannot hear the difference, so context decides. Ein Ehepaar ist verheiratet, ein Paar nicht unbedingt.

example.de: Ein Ehepaar ist verheiratet, ein Paar nicht unbedingt.
example.en: A married couple is married, a couple not necessarily.

cards.more: Think of five drawers. In the first you put the names, in the second the time (seit wann?), in the third the beginning (wie kennengelernt?), in the fourth what the two share, in the fifth what is different. To introduce a couple you open the drawers one after another and say one sentence from each. You never need more than five sentences, and the order always sounds natural to a German listener.

cards.title: Von der ersten Begegnung bis zur Hochzeit
cards.lead: Every couple's story follows the same road. This card gives you six verbs for the stages, so you can tell the story step by step.
cards.body: Six verbs tell a whole love story. Zusammenkommen and zusammenziehen use sein, the others use haben. In a story the earlier stages go into Plusquamperfekt, and the later ones into Präteritum or Perfekt.
steps: 1. sich kennenlernen: Sie haben sich auf einer Party kennengelernt.
2. sich verlieben: Er hat sich in sie verliebt.
3. zusammenkommen: Nach dem Fest sind sie zusammengekommen.
4. zusammenziehen: Dann sind sie zusammengezogen.
5. sich verloben: Später haben sie sich verlobt.
6. heiraten: Im Sommer haben sie geheiratet.

examples.de: Nachdem sie sich verliebt hatten, sind sie zusammengezogen.
examples.en: After they had fallen in love, they moved in together.
examples.why: verlieben with haben in the nachdem-clause, zusammenziehen with sein in the main clause.

examples.de: Bevor sie heirateten, waren sie drei Jahre zusammen.
examples.en: Before they got married, they had been together for three years.
examples.why: bevor: same tense in both parts.

examples.de: Sie haben sich im Sommer verlobt.
examples.en: They got engaged in summer.
examples.why: sich verloben takes haben.

deeper.text: Zusammen sein means to be a couple, zusammenkommen means to become one. The first describes a state, the second a moment: Wir sind seit zwei Jahren zusammen. Wir sind im Mai zusammengekommen. At the end of a relationship Germans say sich trennen, and after a marriage sich scheiden lassen. Just recognise these two.

example.de: Wir sind seit zwei Jahren zusammen.
example.en: We have been together for two years.

cards.more: Walk along a path with six stones. On the first stone you meet each other, on the second your heart jumps, on the third you officially become a couple, on the fourth you share a key, on the fifth you put on a ring, on the sixth you say yes in front of everyone. Each stone is one verb. You can skip stones: not every couple gets engaged. But the order of the verbs always stays the same.

cards.title: Zwei berühmte Paare
cards.lead: Now two real couples from history. Their stories use exactly the tools of this chapter, so read them for content and for tenses.
cards.body: Clara and Robert Schumann and Marie and Pierre Curie are famous in Germany and in Europe. Das Gericht means court. Der Physiker is a physicist. Look at hatte and war: they show what happened earlier.
steps: Clara und Robert Schumann: Clara war eine berühmte Pianistin, Robert war Komponist. Claras Vater war gegen die Heirat. Nachdem ein Gericht sie erlaubt hatte, heirateten sie 1840.
Marie und Pierre Curie: Beide waren Physiker in Paris. 1903 bekamen sie gemeinsam mit einem Kollegen den Nobelpreis für Physik.

examples.de: Clara Schumann war eine berühmte Pianistin, Robert war Komponist.
examples.en: Clara Schumann was a famous pianist, Robert was a composer.
examples.why: Jobs have no article after sein.

examples.de: Nachdem ein Gericht die Heirat erlaubt hatte, heirateten sie 1840.
examples.en: After a court had allowed the marriage, they married in 1840.
examples.why: The permission came first, so Plusquamperfekt.

examples.de: Marie und Pierre Curie bekamen 1903 gemeinsam mit einem Kollegen den Nobelpreis für Physik.
examples.en: In 1903, Marie and Pierre Curie received the Nobel Prize in Physics together with a colleague.
examples.why: Dativ after mit: einem Kollegen.

deeper.text: Clara Schumann is so well known in Germany that her portrait was printed on the 100-Mark banknote before the euro came. A woman on the money: that says a lot about how much people respected her as a pianist. Her father had wanted something else, but the music and the marriage won in the end.

example.de: Ihr Bild war früher auf dem 100-Mark-Schein.
example.en: Her picture used to be on the 100-mark note.

cards.more: Both stories share a pattern: two people, one shared passion and one big moment. Clara and Robert had to fight for their marriage, because her father said no. Marie and Pierre worked side by side in physics, and the prize came to both. German texts about couples usually go through time, so Plusquamperfekt and Präteritum appear together. When you read such a text, underline the hatte and war forms first: they are the flashbacks.

cards.title: Über ein berühmtes Paar sprechen
cards.lead: With the two stories in your head you can build your own short talk. Four steps in a fixed order make it easy.
cards.body: Tell in four steps: who they are, how they met, what they did together, why they are famous. Start the second step with nachdem and a Plusquamperfekt clause, and the rest comes in Präteritum.
steps: 1. Wer? Das waren Marie und Pierre Curie.
2. Wie kennengelernt? Sie lernten sich in Paris kennen, nachdem Marie dort ihr Studium begonnen hatte.
3. Was gemeinsam? Sie arbeiteten gemeinsam im Labor.
4. Warum berühmt? Sie bekamen den Nobelpreis.

examples.de: Sie lernten sich in Paris kennen, nachdem Marie dort ihr Studium begonnen hatte.
examples.en: They met in Paris after Marie had started her studies there.
examples.why: Starting the studies came first: Plusquamperfekt.

examples.de: Beide arbeiteten gemeinsam im Labor.
examples.en: Both worked together in the lab.
examples.why: gemeinsam = together, as a team.

examples.de: Sie sind berühmt, weil sie den Nobelpreis bekommen haben.
examples.en: They are famous because they received the Nobel Prize.
examples.why: weil + Perfekt: haben at the end.

deeper.text: Beide means both and works like a plural pronoun: Beide waren Physiker. Die beiden is the same idea with a stronger feeling of these two together: Die beiden waren ein gutes Team. And beides, with an s, means both things: Beides ist wahr. Say beide for people and beides for two things.

example.de: Die beiden waren ein gutes Team.
example.en: The two of them were a good team.

cards.more: Imagine you tell the story to a friend over a coffee. First you say who you mean, so the friend knows the people. Then comes the little flashback that explains how they got to know each other. After that the story moves forward, and at the end you give the reason why anyone still talks about them. Four steps, four sentences. Practise them with any famous couple you like, and your talk will always have a clear shape.

cards.title: Dein Paar: ein Beispieltext
cards.lead: Last step: your own turn. Here is a model text about a couple you might know. Read it, then replace the details with your own.
cards.body: The model uses one nachdem-clause with Plusquamperfekt and one seitdem-clause with Präsens. Change the names, the places and the time, but keep the frame. Two sayings at the end make the text sound alive.
steps: Das sind meine Eltern. Sie sind seit dreißig Jahren verheiratet.
Sie haben sich beim Studium kennengelernt.
Nachdem sie zwei Jahre zusammen gewesen waren, haben sie geheiratet.
Seitdem sie in Hamburg wohnen, haben sie viele Freunde gefunden.
Gemeinsam ist ihnen die Liebe zum Wandern. Gegensätze ziehen sich an: Er ist ruhig, und sie ist laut.

examples.de: Nachdem sie zwei Jahre zusammen gewesen waren, haben sie geheiratet.
examples.en: After they had been together for two years, they got married.
examples.why: gewesen waren: Plusquamperfekt of sein.

examples.de: Seitdem sie in Hamburg wohnen, haben sie viele Freunde gefunden.
examples.en: Since they have lived in Hamburg, they have found many friends.
examples.why: Still true today, so Präsens after seitdem.

examples.de: Gegensätze ziehen sich an.
examples.en: Opposites attract.
examples.why: A saying: learn it as one block.

deeper.text: Two more useful phrases for couples: Sie ergänzen sich gut means they complement each other, one is strong where the other is weak. Sie passen gut zusammen means they suit each other. Both are positive and you can say them in a toast or in a speech at a wedding.

example.de: Sie passen gut zusammen.
example.en: They suit each other well.

cards.more: Think of a recipe card. The frame is the recipe: names, time, beginning, shared things, differences. The details are the ingredients and you swap them freely. Your parents, your neighbours or a pair of friends fit just as well as Marie and Pierre. Keep the two clauses with nachdem and seitdem, because they show the listener that you can order events in time. Then close with a saying, and you finish like a native speaker.
